Lesson 25: When the best cornerback is out: who covers the star receiver

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked tonight and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files (and the original football-film-room repository isn't reachable from this run). So this lesson adds a new concept that tonight's game is built around: Denver will play Seattle (Thu 5:15 p.m. PT) without its best cornerback, Pat Surtain II, or starting safety Talanoa Hufanga, and Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba has 100+ receiving yards in 4 of 5 games.

The big idea: every defense has to answer one question about the other team's best receiver: who covers him? With a star cornerback, the answer is easy: he follows that receiver everywhere ("shadows" him), one on one, and the other ten defenders play normally. Take the star corner away and the defense has two choices, and each one costs something.

White = offense, yellow = defense. WR wide receiver ("star WR" is the offense's best; "other WR" is the next one) · CB cornerback · S safety · QB quarterback · white squares = offensive linemen. Dashed white arrow = the star's route. Yellow arrow = the safety moving over before or at the snap.

  1. Picture A, backup alone: the next cornerback covers the star one-on-one and the safety (S) stays in the middle of the field. Denver's options are Riley Moss (questionable, ribs) and Josh Jobe (PFF grade 54.1 this season). The cost: the offense's best player gets single coverage from a weaker defender all game.
  2. Picture B, bracket (two on one): the cornerback plays underneath (takes the short throw) and a safety rotates over the top (takes the deep throw), so the star has a defender on both sides. The cost: that safety has left the middle, so the other receiver ("other WR") is one-on-one and the middle of the field is open for runs and tight ends.
  3. How you spot it before the snap: it's Lesson 20 (read the safeties) with one more question. Two safeties split evenly = no special help. Two safeties, but one shaded toward the star's side = a bracket is likely: the defense just told you who it fears.
  4. Why it decides games: once the star is bracketed, the offense's second and third options have to win. Seattle's are thin (Smith-Njigba has about half of Seattle's receiving yards, per TheSpread). That's why the brief still likes Denver +3.5 without Surtain: Picture B makes Seattle beat Denver with someone else.

Real examples:

  • Picture A gone wrong: USC 31, Penn State 23 (Oct 10). Penn State played without three cornerbacks, so it had nobody to bracket with. Jayden Maiava threw for 301 yards and 3 TDs (210 by halftime) and Trent Mosley caught 9 for 111.
  • A different choice: Bills 37, Rams 34 (Oct 12). Buffalo played zone about 78% of the time instead of doubling Puka Nacua. He caught a Monday-night-record 17 passes on 24 targets, but for 138 yards, about 8 a catch: zone gave up the short catches and took away the big ones. Defenses choose which damage to accept.
  • Tonight's tell: on Seattle's first third down, does a Denver safety drift toward Smith-Njigba before the snap (Picture B), or stay centered (Picture A)? VSiN expects Denver to load up against the run instead, which would mean more Picture A, the best case for Smith-Njigba.

Connecting the dots: shadowing is Lesson 5's man coverage aimed at one player; a bracket is a Cover 2 idea (Lesson 8) used on one side of the field; Lesson 9's bunched receivers are how offenses make brackets hard (who does the safety help on when three receivers stand together?). And Lesson 19's box count tells you what the defense gave up to send that safety over.

For your Film Room drill: before each snap, find the offense's best receiver and the nearest safety. Safety shaded toward him + six or fewer in the box = the defense chose the bracket and gave up the run: lean RUN (or a throw to the other side). Safety centered, the star split wide by himself, passing down = one-on-one: lean PASS, toward the star. Log "bracket" or "1-on-1" with your call, so the review can check it.

Video: search YouTube for "bracket coverage explained NFL" and "shadow cornerback explained."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 3: Safeties & coverages)

Lesson 26: Overtime: how NFL and college OT work (and why it counts for your bets)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked tonight and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files (the original football-film-room repository isn't reachable from this run). So there's no miss of yours to fix, and this lesson takes a new concept from last night instead: both of Thursday's games went to overtime, and they used two completely different sets of rules. It also matters for betting: UAB-ECU's total went from 34 to 47 in overtime.

The big idea: overtime is a mini-game with its own rules. In the NFL, both teams get a chance with the ball (in the regular season since 2025), then the next score wins, inside a 10-minute clock. In college there is no clock at all: each team gets one possession from the opponent's 25-yard line, over and over, until one side is ahead after both have had the ball.

Left: Thursday's Broncos-Seahawks overtime. Right: Thursday's UAB-East Carolina overtime. Each box is one step; the yellow box ended the game. PAT = point after touchdown (extra point). INT = interception.

  1. NFL, step by step (left): a coin toss decides who gets the ball. Seattle won it and drove, but Ja'Quan McMillian intercepted Sam Darnold on 3rd-and-7. Under the old rule, a Seattle field goal on that first drive would have let Denver answer, but a Seattle touchdown would have ended it; now even a first-drive touchdown gives the other team a turn. Once both teams have had the ball, the next score of any kind wins: Denver's drive ended with Wil Lutz's 53-yard field goal, 17-14.
  2. If nobody scores in 10 minutes, an NFL regular-season game ends in a tie, which is how Giants-Commanders finished 27-27 last Sunday (the brief's Giants +3.5 won on it).
  3. College, step by step (right): UAB went first from ECU's 25 and scored (Ryder Burton's 6-yard TD to Rod Robinson II, plus the extra point: 24-17). ECU then had to score a touchdown from UAB's 25 to keep playing. Emory Williams threw an interception and Delvon Gulley ran it back 80 yards. ECU's possession was over, so the game was over, and the return touchdown still counted: 30-17.
  4. College's 2-point rules: from the 2nd overtime, a team that scores a touchdown must go for 2 (no kick). From the 3rd overtime on, there are no drives at all, just one 2-point play per team, back and forth. That's why long college overtimes end with scores like 61-58.
  5. Why the coin toss choice differs: in college, the toss winner almost always chooses defense first, so it knows exactly what it needs when its turn comes (the recaps don't say who won Thursday's toss; UAB going first suggests ECU made that choice). In the NFL, taking the ball first is usually right now, because you're guaranteed a second possession if the game is still tied after both teams have had it.

Real examples:

  • Bills 37, Rams 34 (Oct 12): Buffalo got the ball first in overtime, and James Cook fumbled at the Rams' 20. The Rams drove to Buffalo's 30, but Greg Rousseau blocked Harrison Mevis' 48-yard try. Both teams had now had the ball, so Tyler Bass's 45-yarder on the next drive ended it. Same rule as Thursday.
  • Why the NFL changed the rule: in the January 2022 playoffs, the Chiefs beat the Bills 42-36 on the first overtime drive and Josh Allen never touched the ball. The league guaranteed both teams a possession in the playoffs the next year, and in the regular season starting in 2025.
  • Betting, from UAB-ECU: the total was 47.5. Regulation ended 17-17 (34 points); overtime added 13; final 47, so the Under won by half a point. UAB +4.5 won too. Sportsbooks count overtime for spreads, totals and player props, and Kalshi's game, spread and total markets follow the official final (check the rules line on any contract). An Under bettor at 34 points with the score tied is not safe yet.

Connecting the dots: overtime is the two-minute drill (Lessons 11 and 23) with no clock in college, and the red zone (Lesson 12) every time: college OT starts at the 25, just outside it. Kicking matters more than anywhere else (Lesson 4): Lutz's 53-yarder won Thursday; Mevis' blocked 48-yarder lost Monday.

For your Film Room drill: in overtime, ask what the offense needs before you call run or pass. Team going second in college, down 7: it can't kick, so long downs lean PASS and 4th down is a go. NFL team that only needs a field goal, already in range: lean RUN (protect the ball, center it for the kicker), like Denver's drive before Lutz's kick. Log "OT: needs TD" or "OT: needs FG" with your call.

Video: search YouTube for "NFL overtime rules 2025 explained" and "college football overtime rules explained."

Lesson 27: Backup quarterbacks: how the game plan shrinks (and how to call it in your drill)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked tonight and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files, and the original football-film-room repository isn't reachable from this run. So there's no miss of yours to fix, and this lesson takes a new concept straight from this weekend: backup quarterbacks are starting everywhere. Friday, Washington won at Purdue with its backup. This weekend: Tanner McKee for Jalen Hurts (Eagles), Tyler Huntley for Lamar Jackson (Ravens), Jalon Daniels for Baker Mayfield (Bucs), maybe Tyson Bagent for Caleb Williams (Bears), and in college Ty Dieffenbach (UCLA), George MacIntyre (Tennessee) and Trammel Jones (Florida).

The big idea: a coach doesn't hand a backup the starter's whole playbook. The backup has had fewer practice snaps with the first team, and the coach trusts him less with risky throws. So the plan shrinks: more runs, more quick, short throws the quarterback can make on his first read, and fewer deep shots and long-developing plays. For your drill, that means a backup shifts your run/pass calls toward RUN on early downs.

Left: a starter's menu reaches all three passing depths (dashed = passes) plus normal runs (solid). Right: with a backup, thick arrows = used more (runs and quick short throws), thin dotted = used less (middle and deep). This is a schematic of the usual pattern, not a measured chart; the real examples below show it.

  1. More runs (bottom of the right panel): handing off is the safest play a backup can run, and it keeps the defense from teeing off on him. Last week (Thu Oct 8) Tampa started Jalon Daniels at Dallas and ran for 241 yards in a 24-16 upset. Last Sunday Baltimore started Tyler Huntley at Atlanta and ran the ball behind Derrick Henry: 111 rushing yards by halftime, and Baltimore had the ball 19:28 to Atlanta's 10:32 in the first half.
  2. Quick, safe throws (short zone): passes that come out in about two seconds to the first receiver he looks at (slants, hitches, screens: Lesson 16's play-action helps too). These cut down sacks and interceptions, which is what the coach fears most.
  3. Fewer middle and deep throws (top zones): throws over the middle and deep need the quarterback to read safeties (Lesson 20) and trust timing with his receivers. Backups get fewer of those calls, so the defense can creep closer to the line, which is why a backup's team often struggles to run even while trying to run more.
  4. When it breaks the pattern: some backups get the full menu and play well, and the defense baits them into mistakes anyway. Friday, Washington's Elijah Brown (starting for the injured Demond Williams Jr.) threw for 302 yards and 3 TDs on 28 passes, and also 3 interceptions. Washington still won 38-26 because Trey Cooley ran 8 times for 113 yards (runs of 43 and 53) and Purdue couldn't run at all.
  5. Why the betting market cares: the quarterback is the biggest single swing in a point spread. When Hurts was ruled out (a blood clot in his calf) along with Saquon Barkley, Eagles-Panthers flipped from Eagles -1.5 to Panthers -3.5 and the total fell to about 39. Mississippi State-LSU moved from LSU -10.5 to -15.5 once QB Kamario Taylor was listed doubtful. Backups also pull totals down: fewer deep shots, more clock-eating runs.

Real examples to watch this weekend:

  • Tennessee's George MacIntyre vs. Alabama (Sat 12:30 p.m. PT, ABC): NBC/Yahoo's pick is the Under because both teams are expected to lean on the run.
  • UCLA's Ty Dieffenbach vs. Wisconsin (Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC): Nico Iamaleava is out for the season; the line dropped from UCLA -3.5 to -2.5.
  • Eagles' Tanner McKee vs. Carolina (Sun 10:00 a.m. PT, CBS) and Ravens' Tyler Huntley at Cleveland (same time, FOX): count how often each team runs on 1st down in the first quarter.
  • It helps the other team's running back too: if the Bears start Tyson Bagent instead of Caleb Williams, Atlanta is likelier to lead late, and a team that leads runs, which is part of why the brief picked Bijan Robinson 70+ this week.

Connecting the dots: this is game script (Lesson 23) chosen before kickoff instead of forced by the score. It shows up in the box count (Lesson 19): defenses put an 8th player near the line against a backup because they fear the run more than the pass. And it ties to pass protection (Lesson 24): quick throws are how a coach protects a backup without extra blockers.

For your Film Room drill: before the first snap, note whether a backup is starting (the broadcast always says so). Then: 1st and 10 or 2nd and medium → lean RUN more than you normally would; 3rd and 7+ → still PASS (even a backup has to throw then, usually short, at or just past the sticks); leading in the 2nd half → RUN. Watch the first two drives: if the backup completes a couple of throws past 15 yards, the coach will open the playbook and you should move back toward your normal calls. Log "backup QB" in your notes so the review can check the pattern.

Lesson 28: The strip-sack: why one swipe at the ball decided Saturday's biggest games

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files (the original football-film-room repository isn't reachable from this run). So there's no miss of yours to fix, and this lesson takes a new concept straight from Saturday's noon games, where a strip-sack or a sack-fumble showed up in three of the four big finals.

The big idea: a strip-sack is a sack where the rusher knocks the ball out instead of (or while) tackling the quarterback. It almost always comes from the quarterback's blind side, the side he isn't facing when he sets up to throw: for a right-handed quarterback, that's his left. The rusher who gets there is usually the edge rusher lined up outside the left tackle. The ball is easiest to knock loose at one moment: when the quarterback has one hand on it with his arm cocked back to throw.

Top-down view, offense moving up the screen. The edge rusher (yellow X) starts outside the left tackle on the blind side, loops around him (dashed path) and arrives behind the quarterback, reaching for the ball in his right hand. Bottom boxes: when the ball is exposed vs. safe.

  1. Why the blind side (left of the picture): a right-handed quarterback drops back facing slightly right, so he can't see a rusher coming from his left. He never braces or tucks the ball. That's why the left tackle protecting that side is usually one of the best-paid players on an offense (Lesson 24 counted blockers vs. rushers; this is the one matchup inside that count that matters most).
  2. Why the arm cocked back (EXPOSED box): in the pocket, a good quarterback holds the ball with both hands, high and tight (SAFE box). To throw, he has to take one hand off and pull the ball back behind his ear. For that split second it's held by one hand, away from his body. A rusher arriving from behind doesn't tackle first: he chops or swipes down at that arm.
  3. Why it swings games (bottom line): a loose ball bouncing on the turf is close to a coin flip for who gets it, and the defense often recovers near the quarterback, which is deep in the offense's own territory. So one swipe turns a normal drive into a short field for the other team (Market 101 Lesson 9: turnovers and short fields).

Saturday's real examples:

  • Ohio State 19, Indiana 15 (Sat 9:00 a.m. PT): Indiana had one turnover all season, then lost fumbles on its first two drives of the second half. The second one was Josh Hoover sacked and fumbling in Ohio State territory, a scoring chance turned into an Ohio State possession. Ohio State won by 4.
  • Florida 27, Texas 24: Florida sacked Arch Manning 5 times, and the game ended when Myles Graham forced a Manning fumble with 1:58 left (Kanye Clark recovered) while Texas was trying to tie or win it. A three-point game, decided by one swipe.
  • Northwestern 24, Michigan State 21: Northwestern's Michael Kilbane strip-sacked the quarterback and recovered it himself, in a game won on a field goal with 5 seconds left.
  • Alabama at Tennessee (live): Alabama's Keelon Russell lost a fumble on a sack in the first half; a return touchdown was overturned (ruled down), but Tennessee kept the ball.
  • Watch Sunday: Chicago's pass rush is thin (Montez Sweat suspended, Dayo Odeyingbo on IR) against Michael Penix Jr. (ribs), Sun 10:00 a.m. PT, FOX; and Tanner McKee, a backup who completes 41.9% under pressure per Sharp Football, faces Carolina, same time, CBS.

Connecting the dots: pass protection (Lesson 24) decides whether a rusher gets free; this lesson is what happens when one does. A backup quarterback (Lesson 27) holds the ball longer while reading, which is more time with the ball exposed, so coaches give backups quick throws. And a turnover creates a sudden change: the new offense starts on a short field, which takes you straight into the red zone (Lesson 12).

For your Film Room drill: (1) On 3rd and long, check the edge rusher outside the left tackle: if the defense puts its best pass rusher there and the offense leaves the left tackle alone with no tight end or back to help, expect a quick PASS (the coach knows the clock is short). (2) After a strip-sack or any takeaway, the first play for the new offense is often a deep shot, frequently play-action (Lesson 16): the defense that just gave up the ball is rattled and the coach wants to strike. Call PASS on that first snap and log "sudden change" in your notes so the review can check it.

Lesson 29: Kicks are live balls: muffed punts, blocked punts and the onside kick

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was not reachable from this run (access denied). So there's no miss of yours to fix, and this lesson takes a new concept from the weekend, when a muffed punt, a blocked punt and a recovered onside kick each changed a game.

The big idea: on a normal play only the offense has the ball. On a kick, the ball is in the air between two teams, and the rules decide who is allowed to grab it. Most of the time the receiving team simply catches it. But a kick that is touched and dropped, blocked, or kicked short on purpose becomes a loose ball that either team can win, and that's a turnover that doesn't show up as one in the offense's stats.

Top, an onside kick seen from above: white = the kicking team (K kicker, KT kicking-team players) at its own 35; yellow = the receiving team's hands team (HT) just past the 45. The yellow line is the 10-yard mark. Bottom: three punt rules.

  1. The onside kick (top). The kicker (K) kicks the ball along the ground on purpose, short. In college it must travel 10 yards (from the own 35 to the 45, the yellow line) before the kicking team (KT) may recover it, unless a receiving player touches it first. The receiving team sends out its hands team (HT): receivers and backs who catch for a living. Most onside kicks fail, and a team that recovers one gets the ball near midfield. In the NFL a team must announce an onside kick, and only a team that's behind may try one.
  2. The muff (bottom left). A punt returner who touches the ball without catching it makes it a live ball, and the punting team can recover it. They get it where they recover it (they can't run with it). That's why returners let bouncing punts go: touching it is the mistake.
  3. The fair catch (bottom middle). A returner who waves one hand above his head can't be hit; the ball is dead where he catches it. It gives up the return to protect the ball.
  4. The blocked punt (bottom right). A punt blocked behind the line of scrimmage is a loose ball that either team can pick up and run with, like a fumble. A punter is usually standing 13–15 yards deep, so a block often happens deep in the punting team's territory.

This weekend's real examples:

  • Bears 31, Falcons 23 (Sun 10:00 a.m. PT): Atlanta returner Zachariah Branch muffed a punt just before halftime; Chicago recovered and scored to make it 21-7. That lead is what took the ball away from Bijan Robinson (9 carries) and lost the brief's 70+ pick. Branch fumbled a second punt later.
  • Titans 26, Colts 20: down 13-0 at the half, Tennessee scored 20 in the 4th quarter, and one of the TDs was Femi Oladejo's 14-yard return of a blocked punt. Tennessee's first win of the season.
  • Michigan 21, Penn State 18 (Sat 12:30 p.m. PT): after Rocco Becht's 24-yd TD to Chase Sowell with 1:11 left, Penn State needed an onside kick. Michigan's hands team recovered it at its own 49, and a Jordan Marshall 8-yard run got the first down that ended the game. The brief's Penn State +6.5 still won.
  • Florida 27, Texas 24 (Saturday): Ryan Niblett's 64-yard punt-return TD was 7 of Florida's 27 points in a 3-point upset.
  • Watch Monday: Commanders at 49ers, Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN. If Washington is close late, the onside kick and the hands team are part of the brief's Commanders +7.5 math.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 4 introduced special teams and Lesson 15 the kickoff rules; this lesson is what happens when the ball comes loose. A recovered kick is a sudden change like the strip-sack (Lesson 28): the new offense starts on a short field, often already in the red zone (Lesson 12). And a failed onside kick hands the leading team the clock: that's the four-minute offense (Lesson 23).

For your Film Room drill: (1) After a failed onside kick the leading team runs to burn clock: call RUN on the next snaps (Michigan ran on every play after recovering). (2) After a muffed punt or blocked punt recovered near the goal line (inside the 10), call RUN (short yardage, Lesson 17); recovered near midfield, the first snap is often a PASS shot, as after a strip-sack. Log "sudden change" in your notes so the review can check it.

Lesson 30: The tight end: half lineman, half receiver, and the matchup defenses can't solve

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no miss of yours to fix. This lesson takes a new concept from Week 6, when tight ends scored or set up the big moments in four games, and from tonight's Monday-night game, where George Kittle is the biggest risk to the brief's Commanders +7.5.

The big idea: the tight end (TE) lines up at the end of the offensive line, so he can block like a sixth lineman or run out for a pass like a receiver. The defense can't tell which from where he stands, and it has no player who matches him well at both jobs: a linebacker is big enough to take on his block but usually too slow to cover him; a safety can run with him but gives up 30–60 pounds.

White = offense (squares = linemen LT, LG, C, RG, RT; Y = inline tight end; TE = flexed tight end; WR receivers; QB; RB). Yellow = defense (DL linemen, LB linebackers, CB cornerbacks, S safeties). Dashed line = line of scrimmage; solid arrow = a block, dashed arrow = a pass route.

  1. Where he lines up. The inline TE (Y) stands right next to the right tackle (RT), usually in a 3-point stance (one hand on the ground) like a lineman. The flexed TE stands a yard or two off the line and outside, upright like a receiver. Some teams split a TE all the way out wide just to see who covers him.
  2. Job 1: block the edge. On an outside run, the inline TE blocks the defensive end (the DL across from him) so the running back can get around the corner. In pass protection he often "chips" that rusher (one quick hit) before running his route: the extra blocker you counted in Lesson 24.
  3. Job 2: the seam route. The flexed TE runs straight up the field between the linebacker and the safety, the "seam." The LB: too slow to stay with him; the S: too small to stop him at the catch. Against zone he sits in the soft spot between them (Lesson 8).
  4. Personnel tells you how many there are (bottom boxes). Lesson 1's numbers: 11 personnel = 1 TE, 12 = 2 TEs, 13 = 3. More tight ends usually make the defense bring in bigger players (base defense, Lesson 2), and that's exactly when play-action (Lesson 16) to a tight end works best.
  5. The red zone. Inside the 20 the field shrinks (Lesson 12), and a 6-foot-5 target who can box out a smaller defender is the easiest throw there. That's why tight ends score so many short touchdowns.

Week 6's real examples:

  • Kyle Pitts (Falcons): 5 catches, 60 yards and 2 TDs in the 31-23 loss to Chicago. Atlanta was throwing to catch up, the same script that sank the brief's Bijan Robinson 70+.
  • Tommy Tremble (Panthers): caught both of Bryce Young's TD passes in the 25-14 win at Philadelphia.
  • Colby Parkinson (Rams): the go-ahead TD from Matthew Stafford with 47 seconds left against Arizona (Arizona still won with a field goal at 0:00).
  • Michael Mayer and Brock Bowers (Raiders): 7-95 (a career high) and 4-70 in the 33-30 loss to Buffalo. Two tight ends on the field together is 12 personnel.
  • Tonight: George Kittle (49ers): 21 catches, 268 yards and 4 TDs through Week 5, and his 56-yard TD sealed the Week 4 win over Denver. Washington has allowed 7 TDs to tight ends; his prop is 63.5 receiving yards and Kalshi's anytime-TD price is about 47¢. With Deebo Samuel out and Mike Evans questionable, more throws should go his way: the main risk to the brief's Commanders +7.5, Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN/ABC.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 1 (personnel) counts the tight ends; Lesson 10 (formations) shows where they stand; Lesson 19 (count the box) explains why an extra inline TE pulls an extra defender into the box; Lesson 22 (motion) is how offenses move the TE before the snap to create the mismatch.

For your Film Room drill: (1) Inline TE with a hand on the ground, especially two or three of them (12 or 13 personnel), in short yardage or the four-minute offense → lean RUN. (2) TE standing up, flexed off the line or split wide → lean PASS. (3) TE motions across the formation right before the snap → he's often going to block the back side of a run, or it's play-action: call RUN unless it's 3rd-and-long. Note the TE's stance next to each call so the review can check which tell you used.

Lesson 31: Protecting a lead: why 20-3 at halftime became 23-17 (and why it matters for the points)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no miss of yours to fix. This lesson takes a new concept from Monday night, when the 49ers nearly lost a 20-point lead and the brief's Commanders +7.5 won on Washington's late touchdowns.

The big idea: once a team leads by two scores or more in the second half, both teams change how they play. The team that's ahead stops trying to score fast and starts trying to use up the clock: its offense runs the ball (the four-minute offense, Lesson 23) and its defense backs off so nothing goes over its head. The team that's behind throws on almost every play. Those two changes together are why big leads so often shrink late, even when the leading team was much better for most of the game.

White = offense (squares = linemen; WR receivers; QB). Yellow = defense (DL linemen, LB linebackers, CB cornerbacks, S safeties). Dashed white line = line of scrimmage; dashed arrows = pass routes. Bottom bars: white = 1st half, yellow = 2nd half.

  1. The deep zone (top band). A defense protecting a big lead puts four defensive backs 20 or more yards deep. Its only goal is to stop a one-play touchdown. A 12-yard catch in front of them is fine: the receiver gets tackled, and the clock keeps running. This is called a "prevent" or soft zone.
  2. Only 3 rushers. To have enough players deep, the defense often rushes just three linemen. With fewer rushers, the quarterback has more time (Lesson 24's counting: more blockers than rushers), so he can complete pass after pass.
  3. Short throws in front. The receivers' routes stop underneath, in the open space between the linebackers and the deep zone. Each one gains 8 to 15 yards. On Monday, nine different Commanders caught a pass and Jayden Daniels finished 29 of 40 for 300 yards, most of it after halftime.
  4. The leader's offense goes quiet. The team that's ahead runs into defenses that know a run is coming (an extra defender in the box, Lesson 19). Short runs, punts, and the other team gets the ball back. San Francisco's last three drives were three-and-outs that gained 7 yards in total.
  5. Yards by half (bottom bars). The 49ers had 303 yards in the first half and 72 in the second; Washington had 90, then 224. Same teams, same night: the score changed how both of them played.

Why it doesn't always work for the trailing team: it's racing the clock, so it needs everything to go right. Washington got help from four 49ers defensive penalties, but on 4th down from the SF 17 Malik Mustapha knocked the ball from Treylon Burks in the end zone, and the last snap was a sack. Leads shrink much more often than they disappear.

Real examples:

  • 49ers 23, Commanders 17 (Monday): 20-3 at the half, 23-3 with 18 seconds left in the 3rd, then two Daniels TD passes. Washington +7.5 covered by a point and a half.
  • Michigan 21, Penn State 18 (Saturday): Michigan led 14-3 after three quarters (two TDs off Penn State interceptions) and scored again in the 4th; Penn State scored 15 in the 4th (Carson Hansen's TD and 2-point pass, then Rocco Becht to Chase Sowell for 24 yards with 1:11 left). Michigan recovered the onside kick. Penn State +6.5 covered.
  • Bills 33, Raiders 30 (Sunday): Tre Tucker's 44-yard TD with 1:32 left made it a 3-point game; Las Vegas +4.5 to +5.5 covered.
  • The other way: Titans 26, Colts 20 (Sunday): Indianapolis led 13-0 at the half and lost; Tennessee scored 20 in the 4th, including a blocked-punt return TD. Sometimes the lead doesn't just shrink.

What it means for your bets: a late touchdown by a team that's losing anyway changes nothing about who wins, but it can flip the spread. Bettors call that a "backdoor cover." When you take the points (Commanders +7.5, Penn State +6.5), garbage-time scoring works for you; when you lay a big number with a favorite, it works against you. It also matters live: a 17-point halftime lead tends to be smaller by the end, so a live price that assumes the leader keeps scoring at the same rate is usually too high (Market 101, Lesson 8).

Connecting the dots: Lesson 23 (the clock changes the call) is the leading team's side of this; Lesson 24 (count blockers vs. rushers) explains why a 3-man rush gives the quarterback time; Lesson 8 (zone coverage) explains why the open space is underneath; Lesson 19 (count the box) is why the leader's runs stop working.

For your Film Room drill: (1) Team ahead by 10+ in the second half, clock running → lean RUN, even on 2nd and 8. (2) Team behind by 10+ in the 4th quarter → PASS on almost every down. (3) Defense shows 3 linemen with safeties very deep → it's sitting on a lead; expect a short pass underneath. Write the score and quarter next to each call so the review can check whether the situation, not the formation, made the call.

Lesson 32: The middle of the line: why backup guards matter more than you'd think

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning and still has no reviewed snaps: the only logged game, Eagles at Bears (Week 3), has 0 saved snaps and there are no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no miss of yours to fix. This lesson takes a new concept from Thursday night: New England plays Chicago with its third- and fourth-string guards, and that's the football reason behind the brief's Under 50.5.

The big idea: fans watch the tackles, who block the fast pass rushers on the outside. But the two guards and the center protect the most important spot on the field: the space right in front of the quarterback. Pressure from the outside, the quarterback can escape by stepping forward. Pressure up the middle, he has nowhere to go. That's why a team can survive a backup tackle more easily than two backup guards.

White squares = offensive linemen (yellow squares = backup guards). Yellow dots = defenders. Solid yellow arrow = linebacker blitzing the A gap; dashed yellow arrow = defensive tackle looping on a twist. Dashed white line = line of scrimmage. Bottom: the Patriots' guard situation for Thursday night.

  1. The gaps (labels on the line). Every space between two linemen has a letter. The A gaps are on either side of the center; the B gaps are between each guard and tackle (Lesson 14 used the same letters for run defense). Guards are responsible for the A and B gaps, the shortest path to the quarterback.
  2. Step up (the dashed line behind the center). Against edge rushers, a quarterback "steps up" into the pocket, and the rushers run past him. That escape only works if the middle holds. A rusher through the A gap arrives in about 2 seconds and closes it, so the throw has to come out early or not at all.
  3. The twist, or stunt (dashed yellow arrow). Two defensive linemen swap lanes after the snap: one charges at a guard, the other loops behind him into the gap next door. Beating it takes two blockers who trust each other to "pass off" the defenders. Backup guards who haven't practiced together (and on a Thursday they've had 3 days, Market 101 Lesson 28) are the classic victims.
  4. The A-gap blitz (solid yellow arrow). A linebacker walks up over the center and runs straight through. If the center and guards are busy with the twist, nobody is left for him (Lesson 24's counting: more rushers than blockers in one spot).
  5. Who plays Thursday (bottom panel). New England has lost four guards: Mike Onwenu and Greg Van Roten (IR), Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and Ben Brown (knee), both ruled out Wednesday. Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor start. RT Morgan Moses is questionable, and rookie Caleb Lomu played 59 snaps at right tackle last week.

How offenses hide a weak middle: quick throws (the ball out before the twist gets home), screens (let the rushers in on purpose and throw over them), runs to the outside instead of up the middle, and keeping a tight end or running back in to block, which means one fewer receiver. Every one of those shrinks the playbook, which is the case for fewer points (and for an Under).

Real examples:

  • Patriots at Bears (Thursday): New England's backup guards against a Chicago defense that's top-10 in EPA per play and has 42 takeaways since the start of last season. Drake Maye has thrown 10 TDs and 1 INT in his last three starts, so this is the test of whether that holds with a patched middle.
  • The counterexample: Michigan 21, Penn State 18 (Saturday): Michigan played without OL Andrew Sprague and Ace Hamilton, with three more linemen questionable, and still ran for 211 yards. A weak line is a reason to expect trouble, not a guarantee, especially for runs, where the blockers move forward instead of holding their ground.
  • Steelers 26, Buccaneers 19 (Sunday): Aaron Rodgers was sacked 5 times; the last one, by Jalen Ramsey on 4th down in overtime, ended the game. Inside pressure on a quarterback who doesn't move much is the hardest kind to escape.

What it means for your bets: an injury report that lists two guards is easy to skip (nobody knows the names), which is why it can matter more than the price shows. Pass-heavy props for a quarterback behind backup guards get riskier; Unders get a reason. But check the other side too: Thursday's game has a reason for the Under (New England's guards) and a reason for the Over (New England's three missing cornerbacks). The brief's estimate is only a small edge because both are real.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 24 (count blockers vs. rushers) explains why an extra rusher in one gap gets free; Lesson 6 (the blitz) is the gamble the defense takes to make it happen; Lesson 14 (gaps) is the same map used for runs; Lesson 28 (the strip-sack) is what happens when pressure arrives before the quarterback can protect the ball.

For your Film Room drill: (1) Offense with backup interior linemen, 3rd and 6+ → expect a quick PASS (screen or short throw), not a deep drop-back. (2) Linebacker walked up over the center before the snap → blitz likely; the call is still PASS, but expect it out fast. (3) 1st and 10 with an extra tight end or back staying in → lean RUN or play-action, since the offense is adding blockers. Note the down, distance and who's playing guard next to each call so the review can check whether the line, not the formation, decided it.

Lesson 33: Quarterback runs: designed runs, scrambles and sneaks (and how to log each in your drill)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds only one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix. This lesson covers a call that trips up almost everyone in the drill: when the quarterback ends up running, was it a run play or a pass play? It's live this week: Tommy Carr's legs won Michigan the Penn State game and got him the start against Indiana, and Kalshi prices Drake Maye to run in a touchdown tonight.

The big idea: the box score counts every quarterback run the same way, as a "rush." But there are three very different plays behind those numbers. Two are called runs (the designed run and the sneak). One is a called pass that broke down (the scramble). Your drill asks what the offense called before the snap, so the scramble is a PASS even though the stat sheet says rush.

White = offense (squares are linemen), yellow = defense. Solid arrows = blockers and receivers; dashed white arrow = the quarterback's path. Dashed horizontal line = line of scrimmage. Each panel's "Log" label is how to score it in your Film Room drill.

  1. Designed run (panel 1). The play is built for the quarterback to carry it. In a QB draw, the line first sets up like it's pass blocking, so the linebackers drop back into coverage; then the running back becomes a lead blocker through the A gap and the quarterback follows. Other designed runs: the QB power, and the read option from Lesson 21 when the QB keeps it. Log it as RUN.
  2. Scramble (panel 2). A pass play: the receivers run routes, the line pass-blocks. The edge rush collapses the pocket (Lesson 24), nobody is open, and the quarterback escapes and runs. Log it as PASS, because that was the call. In the drill review, a scramble you logged as PASS is a hit, even though the play shows up in the box score as a rush.
  3. QB sneak (panel 3). Third or fourth down and about a yard. The quarterback lines up under center, takes the snap and pushes straight ahead behind the center into the A gap (Lesson 32's map). It's the highest-percentage short-yardage play in football; the Eagles' "tush push" version, with teammates shoving from behind, is the famous one. Log it as RUN.

Pre-snap clues for each: a mobile quarterback in shotgun with one back beside him and a light box (Lesson 19) → designed run or read option is possible. Quarterback under center, tight formation, 1 yard to go → sneak. Empty backfield, receivers spread wide, 3rd and long → it's a pass, and any QB run will be a scramble.

Real examples:

  • Michigan 21, Penn State 18 (last Saturday): freshman Tommy Carr came in at halftime, went 5 of 7 for 47 yards and ran for 36 yards, including the winning touchdown. Michigan is starting him against Indiana (Sat 9:00 a.m. PT, FOX) partly because a quarterback who can run gives a defense one more ball carrier to account for.
  • 49ers 23, Commanders 17 (Monday): the brief's pregame case leaned on Jayden Daniels running. He ran 4 times for 10 yards. San Francisco's rushers stayed in their lanes instead of flying upfield, which closes the scramble escape in panel 2; Daniels beat them with his arm instead (300 yards).
  • Patriots at Bears (tonight, Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime): Kalshi prices "Drake Maye: rushing touchdown" at about 20¢. With backup guards (Lesson 32), Maye is more likely to scramble than usual, and Chicago is missing linebackers T.J. Edwards (doubtful) and Jack Sanborn (out), the players who usually spy a running quarterback.
  • Eagles (Monday night): with Jalen Hurts out and Tanner McKee, a pocket passer, starting, expect far fewer designed QB runs and sneaks from Philadelphia, one reason the line moved 7.5 points (today's Market 101).

What it means for your bets: a quarterback's rushing-yards prop mixes designed runs (predictable: the coach calls them) and scrambles (unpredictable: they depend on the pass rush). Backup offensive lines and missing spy linebackers raise scramble yards; a disciplined rush that stays in its lanes lowers them, as Monday showed. And a "rushing yards" over for a quarterback is partly a bet that his passing plays break down.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 21 (option and RPO) is the designed-run family; Lesson 24 (pass protection) explains why pockets collapse into scrambles; Lesson 32 (the middle of the line) is the map for the sneak; Lesson 19 (count the box) tells you whether a designed QB run has room.

For your Film Room drill: (1) Empty or 3-wide shotgun, 3rd and 7+: call PASS; if the QB ends up running, it's a scramble and your PASS call was right. (2) QB under center, 1 yard to go: call RUN (sneak). (3) Mobile QB in shotgun, one back beside him, 6 or fewer in the box: lean RUN (draw or keeper). When you save a snap where the QB ran, add a note "scramble" or "designed" so the review can grade the call, not the stat line.

Lesson 34: The two-minute drill: the clock, field-goal range and the onside kick

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds only one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson takes a new concept from Thursday night, where 30 of the 54 points that beat the brief's Under came in two short windows: the last 14 seconds of the first half and the last 94 seconds of the game.

The big idea: at the end of each half, football changes. The team with the ball isn't trying to have a "good drive" anymore; it's trying to score before the clock hits 0:00, or to keep the other team from getting the ball back. Three things run the end of every half: the clock, field-goal range and, at the end of a game, the onside kick.

Top: the kick math, using Thursday's two late field goals (white dot = line of scrimmage, yellow dot = the hold). Middle: the end of the first half on a timeline. Bottom: what stops the game clock.

  1. Field-goal range (diagram, part 1). A field goal is kicked from 7 yards behind the line of scrimmage, and the goalposts sit at the back of the 10-yard end zone. So the kick is always the yard line + 17. Cairo Santos's ball was snapped at New England's 41: 41 + 10 + 7 = 58 yards, the longest of his career, with 1:34 left, after he'd missed from 53 earlier. NFL.com said a kick like that had about a 27.6% chance. Most NFL kickers are reliable inside about 50 yards (the opponent's 33), which is why a two-minute drive is aimed at "getting into range" first and a touchdown second. New England's answer, Andy Borregales from 47 (the Chicago 30), came with 37 seconds left.
  2. The clock (part 3). In the last two minutes the offense lives on plays that stop the clock: an incomplete pass, a run or catch that goes out of bounds, a timeout, or a spike (the quarterback throws the ball straight into the ground on purpose, an incomplete pass that stops the clock without using a timeout). The NFL adds the two-minute warning. In college the clock also stops briefly after a first down, but only in the last two minutes of each half. A completed pass in the middle of the field keeps the clock running, which is why receivers race for the sideline.
  3. Points in a hurry (part 2). Chicago scored with 14 seconds left in the half (Luther Burden, 24 yards) to go up 20-7. That should have ended the half. Instead, after the kickoff, New England got one more snap, and Rhamondre Stevenson caught Drake Maye's pass and went 48 yards for a touchdown on the final play: 20-14. Fourteen seconds, 14 points. This is how totals go over in a hurry (Market 101, Lesson 9).
  4. The onside kick. A team that's behind late can kick off short, hoping to recover the ball itself after it travels at least 10 yards. In the NFL it rarely works, and the kicking team has to announce it under the current kickoff rules. After Borregales's field goal cut it to 30-24 with 37 seconds left, New England tried one; Rome Odunze recovered it for Chicago, and that ended it.
  5. College overtime (a bonus, two games went there Thursday). App State-James Madison and Memphis-East Carolina both went to overtime. In college, each team gets a possession starting at the opponent's 25; from the third overtime on, teams just run alternating two-point plays. That's why college overtime points pile up fast, and why Kalshi totals, which count overtime (Lesson 25), can jump at the end.

How to log it in your drill: in a two-minute drill the offense is almost always passing: log PASS unless you see a clear handoff. A spike is a PASS (it's an intentional incompletion). A kneel-down (the quarterback takes the snap and drops to one knee) is a RUN by the stat sheet; it's the one end-of-game call you can make with certainty before the snap: the leading team in victory formation, everyone bunched tight around the quarterback.

Real examples to look for this weekend: the end of the first half in Indiana at Michigan (Sat 9:00 a.m. PT, FOX): does Michigan, with a freshman quarterback, try to score or run out the clock? And on Sunday, watch for teams at the opponent's 35–40 with under a minute left: that's the line where coaches decide between one more pass and a long field goal.

Video: search YouTube for "two minute drill explained," "how field goal distance is calculated," and "onside kick rules NFL 2026," then watch the last 14 seconds of the first half of Patriots-Bears.

Lesson 35: Gadget plays: the wildcat, the halfback pass and the pitch

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds only one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. It takes a new concept from this weekend instead: three games turned on plays where someone other than the quarterback handled the ball in an unusual way. These are also the plays most likely to fool a pre-snap run/pass call in your drill.

The big idea: most plays are built on the defense knowing who gets the snap (the quarterback) and who can throw (also the quarterback). Gadget plays break one of those two assumptions on purpose. They work because defenses play their tendencies: linebackers fly toward a run, safeties fill in. Used once or twice a game, at the right moment, they get a free touchdown. Overused, the defense waits for them.

White = offense, yellow = defense; the yellow-filled circle is the player with the ball. Top: the wildcat. Bottom: a halfback pass after a pitch.

  1. The wildcat (top of the diagram). The center snaps the ball straight to a running back or receiver lined up about 5 yards deep, and the quarterback lines up wide as a decoy. Why it works: on a normal handoff, the quarterback hands off and stops playing, so the run game is effectively 10 offensive players against 11 defenders. In the wildcat, the runner is the player taking the snap, so every offensive player is a blocker or the runner: 11 against 11. Saturday at South Carolina, Tennessee trailed 17-14 in the second quarter when receiver Mike Matthews took a wildcat snap and ran 8 yards for the touchdown that gave the Vols their first lead, 21-17. (South Carolina's Vicari Swain was also ejected in that half for targeting Matthews.)
  2. The halfback pass (bottom). The quarterback hands or pitches to the running back, who starts running toward the sideline. The linebackers and a safety come up to stop the run (the same trick as play-action, Lesson 16), and the back stops and throws to a receiver behind them. Any player can throw a forward pass, as long as he's behind the line of scrimmage and it's the only forward pass of the play. Friday night at Virginia, Duke running back Nate Sheppard threw a 28-yard touchdown pass with about a minute left: Duke 19, Virginia 16, the winning score.
  3. The pitch, and why it's risky. A pitch (a soft toss to a back running wide, the heart of the option, Lesson 21) travels backward, so it's a backward pass: if it hits the ground, it's a live fumble, and the defense can recover it (Lesson 29: loose balls are live). Michigan's Tommy Carr, making his first start, lost a fumble on a bad pitch in the first quarter against Indiana, one of his two turnovers in a 13-6 overtime loss.
  4. When coaches call them. Near the goal line (where the extra blocker of the wildcat matters most, Lesson 17), late in close games (Duke), and right after a big emotional moment, when a defense is playing fast and aggressive. A team with a running quarterback gets some of the same "11 against 11" math on every play; that's why Lesson 33's designed quarterback runs are so hard to stop.
  5. The rule that kills gadget passes: offensive linemen can't be more than 1 yard downfield in the NFL (3 yards in college) when a forward pass is thrown beyond the line. On a halfback pass, linemen are run-blocking, so they drift downfield: a flag for ineligible man downfield wipes out the play (Lesson 13 covers penalties).

How to log it in your drill: log what the formation tells you before the snap. A wildcat look (no quarterback under center or in the shotgun, a back or receiver deep) is a RUN call; it is a run the large majority of the time. A halfback pass will be scored PASS, so a RUN call on it will show as a miss: that's the play doing its job, not a mistake in your rule. Keep calling RUN on those looks. One clue that helps: a running back lined up deep with an unusually wide split by the receiver on the side he's running away from.

Real examples to look for: the rest of Saturday night (Ole Miss at Texas, Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, ABC) and Sunday's NFL games inside the 5-yard line, where direct snaps to running backs show up most. Monday night, Philadelphia with backup Tanner McKee (Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN/ABC) is the kind of offense that adds a trick play or two to make up for a backup quarterback.

Lesson 37: The screen pass: letting the pass rush in on purpose

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: still one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps), no review files, last updated Oct 12; the original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no miss of yours to fix yet. This lesson picks up Sunday night: Seattle's pass rush held Kansas City to 4.3 yards a play and no red-zone trips, and the play offenses use to punish a rush like that, the screen, scored the longest TD of Denver's win at Arizona. It's also the play most likely to fool you in the drill (it starts as a pass and ends looking like a run).

The big idea: most pass plays try to keep the rushers away from the quarterback. A screen does the opposite: the blockers let the rushers in on purpose, then slip out in front of a running back (or receiver) who catches a short pass behind the line. The defenders who were chasing the quarterback are now behind the play, and the ball carrier has blockers in front of him in open space.

White = offense, yellow = defense. Numbers match the steps below. The ghost circle is where the quarterback started.

  1. The quarterback sells a deep pass (1). He drops back 7 yards, as if waiting for a long route. The deeper he goes, the farther the rushers run, and the more of them end up behind the play.
  2. The linemen let the rushers through, then release (2). The center, right guard and right tackle block for about a count ("one-thousand-one"), let their man go, and run sideways to the flat. That's the tell for a defender: a lineman who stops pushing. Against a team that rushes hard every snap, like Seattle (No. 1 in ESPN's pass-rush win rate), that's exactly the habit a screen uses.
  3. The short throw, behind the line (3). The quarterback lofts the ball over the rushers to the back, who has drifted out to the side. Because the pass is caught behind the line of scrimmage, the linemen are allowed downfield: the "ineligible man downfield" rule (1 yard in the NFL, 3 in college; Lesson 35) only applies to passes thrown beyond the line.
  4. The back follows his blockers (4). Three big linemen against a linebacker and a cornerback in open space: that's how a 2-yard throw becomes a long gain. Sunday at Arizona, Denver's RJ Harvey took a short screen 52 yards for a touchdown (20-6, 3rd quarter); it came on a day both defenses were attacking upfield (Denver's own rush hit Jacoby Brissett 12 times), the kind of game where a screen finds open grass.
  5. Other screens: the bubble (a slot receiver steps back and catches a quick lateral throw while the outside receiver blocks), the tunnel (a receiver cuts inside behind linemen who block outward), and the tight-end screen. All work the same way: give the defense the space it's rushing into, then use it.
  6. Why the Chiefs couldn't fix Sunday night with it. A screen needs the rushers to over-commit. Seattle's linemen won one-on-one without blitzing, and its linebackers stayed home (rookie Nick Emmanwori had 2 pressures and forced the interception while covering). Kansas City finished with 213 yards. When a defense rushes four and covers with seven, there's no empty space for a screen to use. That's the counter to the counter.
  7. For your bets. Screens are why running-back receiving props and "longest reception" props can surprise: one screen can be 50 yards. A team facing a strong pass rush with a backup quarterback (Philadelphia Monday night, with Tanner McKee against Dallas) will throw screens to its back to keep the rush honest, which adds catches but rarely adds carries.

How to log it in your drill: a screen is a PASS, even though it ends with a running back running behind blockers. Pre-snap clues: 2nd- or 3rd-and-long (6+ yards); the back in the shotgun beside the quarterback; the defense showing blitz (linebackers walked up to the line). If you see those together, PASS is the safe call, and a screen is one of the reasons. After the snap, watch the linemen: if they stop pushing and run sideways, it's a screen. When the drill scores it, a screen counts as a pass; if you called RUN because the result looked like a run, that's the play doing its job.

Real examples to look for: Monday night, Cowboys at Eagles (Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN/ABC): watch for Philadelphia screens to Saquon Barkley on 2nd-and-long. Thursday, Panthers at Packers (Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video). Saturday in college, Ohio State at USC (Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC): spread offenses run bubble screens almost every series.

Video: search YouTube for "RJ Harvey screen touchdown Cardinals," "running back screen pass explained," and "bubble screen vs tunnel screen."

Lesson 38: Fourth down: go for it, punt or kick (and how to call it in your drill)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session, and no tool to add it was available). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson picks up Monday night: Dallas pulled away from a 28-21 game after Philadelphia went for it on 4th down deep in its own territory and failed. It also matters for Thursday's pick: Green Bay is 30th in red-zone TD rate, and whether it kicks or goes for it on 4th-and-goal decides how many points go on the board.

The big idea: on 4th down the offense has one play left before the ball changes hands, and three choices: punt (give the ball back but push the other team about 40 yards away), kick a field goal (3 points, if it's close enough), or go for it (keep the drive if you make the yards; if you don't, the other team gets the ball right where you stopped). Two things decide most of it: where you are on the field and how many yards you need. The score and the clock bend both.

Top: the three zones (1–3), for an offense driving left to right; the yellow dot is roughly where Philadelphia went for it Monday. Bottom (4): how often teams make it, by yards needed (rounded, approximate). Numbers match the steps below.

  1. Your own end: punt (1). From your own 20, a punt moves the other team back about 40 yards. A failed try gives them the ball already in field-goal range, so it's usually worth 3 points or more to them. That's what Philadelphia risked Monday: behind in the 4th quarter with a backup quarterback, it gambled deep in its own territory, didn't make it, and Dallas (Brandon Aubrey 3 of 3 on field goals) pulled away. Trailing late changes the math (step 5); it doesn't remove the downside.
  2. No-man's land: go on short yardage (2). Between your own 40 and the opponent's 35, a field goal would be 52 yards or longer (Lesson 36: add 17 to the yard line), and a punt only gains 30 to 35 yards before it rolls into the end zone. That's why modern coaches go for it here on 4th-and-1 or 2. Detroit under Dan Campbell is the best-known example of a team that does this almost every time.
  3. Field-goal range: kick, unless it's 4th-and-1 (3). Inside the opponent's 35, 3 points are close to certain from an NFL kicker. The exception is very short yardage, especially near the goal line: on 4th-and-goal from the 1 or 2, a touchdown is worth 4 more points than the field goal, so many coaches go.
  4. Distance decides the rest (4). Roughly two in three 4th-and-1 tries succeed; by 4th-and-7 or longer, it's closer to one in four. Philadelphia built its 4th-and-1 game around the quarterback sneak with Jalen Hurts (Lesson 33); with Hurts out for the season, that near-automatic play is gone, which is one more reason its 4th downs are riskier now.
  5. The score and clock bend the zones (Lesson 23). A team trailing in the 4th quarter has fewer possessions left, so a punt "costs" more and going for it moves into the punt zone; a team protecting a lead does the opposite and kicks. In college, the same logic holds, but more kickers are shaky from 45+ yards, so the no-man's land is wider.
  6. For your bets. In the red zone, the 4th-down choice is a 4-point swing (touchdown 7 vs. field goal 3), which is often the difference on a total. Green Bay (30th in red-zone TD rate) settling for field goals is part of the Under 47.5 case Thursday; a Green Bay coach going for it on 4th-and-goal works against it. On the spread, a failed try in your own end usually hands the other team 3 points or more.

How to log it in your drill: on 4th-and-1 or less with the quarterback under center and extra tight ends or linemen in (12 or 13 personnel, Lesson 1), call RUN: a sneak or an inside run is the usual play. On 4th-and-3 or longer, or anytime it's shotgun with 3+ receivers, call PASS. If the punt or field-goal unit comes out, note it as special teams; if they then run a fake, that's a gadget play (Lesson 35), and the drill scores it by what actually happened.

Real examples to watch: Thursday, Panthers at Packers (Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video): Green Bay's choices inside the 10. Saturday in college, Ohio State at USC (Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC). Sunday night, Eagles at Commanders (Sun 5:20 p.m. PT, NBC): whether Nick Sirianni still goes for it with McKee at quarterback.

Lesson 39: Protecting a backup tackle: chips, slides and quick throws (and how to read it in your drill)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session, and no tool to add it was available). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson is about Thursday's game: Carolina will start backups at left tackle, left guard and right tackle (Ikem Ekwonu on PUP, Damien Lewis ruled out Wednesday, rookie Monroe Freeling for the injured Taylor Moton), and how an offense hides weak blockers is the heart of the brief's Under 47.5.

The big idea: a pass rusher who beats his blocker in under 3 seconds wrecks a pass play. When a tackle is a backup or a rookie, the offense can't just hope; it sends help. Every helper is a player who isn't running a route, so the offense trades some of its passing threat for time. That trade is visible before and right after the snap, which makes it useful for your drill and for betting.

Diagram: white = offense, yellow = defense. Yellow-outlined squares are the backups (Carolina's LG and RT Thursday). Arrows 1–2 are the helpers, arrow 3 the line's slide, 4 the quarterback's quick drop. Numbers match the steps below.

  1. Tight end chip (1). The tight end lines up just outside the weak tackle. At the snap he hits the defensive end for a beat, knocking him off his path, then slips into a short route. The rusher loses half a second; the offense loses a deep receiver. You'll see it a lot from Carolina's tight ends on Freeling's side Thursday.
  2. Running back chip (2). The back starts beside the quarterback in the shotgun, steps up, punches the same rusher, then leaks to the flat as the quarterback's safety valve. That's why the brief leans "Chuba Hubbard: 15+ receiving yards": a pressured Bryce Young dumps it to his back (Hubbard has 15 of the 21 catches by Carolina running backs).
  3. Slide protection (3). The whole line shifts its assignments toward the weak side, so the guard next to the backup takes the inside rusher and the tackle only has to worry about the outside one. The cost: the other side is left with one-on-one blocks, which is where a smart defense then attacks (a stunt or a blitz from the far side).
  4. Quick throws (4). The simplest fix: a three-step drop and a throw in about 2.5 seconds, before the rush arrives: slants, hitches, quick outs, screens (Lesson 37). Young already faces pressure on 44.3% of drop-backs when defenses rush four or fewer, the NFL's highest rate, and Green Bay pressures on 38.5% without blitzing, 4th (Bettors Insider). Expect lots of short throws.
  5. Why this lowers scoring. Seven blockers mean three receivers; quick throws mean short gains. An offense playing this way needs 10–12 plays to score instead of a few big ones, and every extra play is another chance for a sack, a penalty or a stalled drive. That's the Under's football reason. The risk to it: the defense guesses wrong and a short throw breaks for a long gain (Tetairoa McMillan is the Carolina player who can do that).
  6. The defense's answers. Rush the weak tackle with a stunt (two linemen crossing), overload the side the line didn't slide to, or drop extra defenders into coverage, since only three receivers are out. Green Bay is short its own pieces (Devonte Wyatt questionable, Micah Parsons out), so watch whether it blitzes or trusts four rushers.

How to log it in your drill: on 2nd- or 3rd-and-long, a tight end lined up tight next to a tackle and a back beside the quarterback in the shotgun usually means PASS with extra protection, not a run, even though it looks "heavy." The tell after the snap: the tight end and back stay home (or chip, then release late) while three receivers run. The same tight-end-in-tight look on 1st-and-10 or short yardage, with the quarterback under center, leans RUN (Lesson 1: personnel plus down and distance). When the drill scores a chip-and-release play, it's a pass.

Real examples to watch: Thursday, Panthers at Packers (Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video): Carolina's right side, where Freeling faces Green Bay's edge rushers. Sunday night, Eagles at Commanders (Sun 5:20 p.m. PT, NBC): Philadelphia without RT Lane Johnson. Monday night, Bears at Seahawks (Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN): Seattle with LT Charles Cross doubtful. In college, Ohio State at USC (Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC).

Lesson 40: Explosive plays: why one long catch flips a game (and how to spot the shot play in your drill)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson comes from Thursday night: Green Bay trailed Carolina 10-6 until Christian Watson's 53-yard catch, and then scored 21 straight points.

The big idea: most drives move the ball 4 or 5 yards at a time. An explosive play skips that work. Analysts usually count a pass of 20+ yards or a run of 10+ yards as explosive (some use 12+ for runs). Drives with one end in points far more often, because the offense needs fewer chances to stay on schedule. One explosive play can matter more than ten good ones.

White = offense, yellow = defense. Solid white arrows are routes; the dashed white line is the throw. Yellow dashed arrows: the linebackers moving toward the fake. Numbers 1–4 match the steps below.

  1. 1. Fake the run. The quarterback pretends to hand off (play-action, Lesson 16).2. Linebackers are taught to stop the run, so they take a step forward. That step empties the middle of the field behind them.
  2. 3. Find the one deep safety. In a 1-high shell (Lesson 20), one safety guards the whole deep middle.4. Send two receivers deep on different sides of him. He can only go to one. The other is open, or covered only by a cornerback running with him.
  3. Thursday's example. Green Bay's short game was efficient (Love 23 of 25 on throws out in under 2.5 seconds, but only 177 yards).The points came from the longer throws: 7 of 14 for 154 yards and 2 TDs on throws of 10+ yards (Next Gen Stats via NFL.com). Watson's 53-yarder flipped a 10-6 deficit.
  4. Saturday's examples. Arizona's Noah Fifita hit Isaiah Mizell for a 94-yard TD at Texas Tech after a scramble.Rutgers' backup AJ Surace was 3 of 12 at Michigan, but one throw went 80 yards for a TD: two-thirds of his 123 yards.Runs count too: J'Koby Williams' 64-yard TD for Texas Tech, and Carson Hansen's 42-yard run for Penn State today.
  5. How defenses stop them. Two deep safeties (2-high) "keep the ball in front": they give up short throws and runs to take away the deep shot (Lesson 20).That's why a 2-high shell often means a long, slow drive, and a 1-high shell invites a shot.

How to log it in your drill: on 1st-and-10 or 2nd-and-short, a quarterback under center (or a back right beside him in the shotgun), wide receivers split out wide and one safety deep in the middle is the classic shot setup. Log it PASS, even though the first thing you see is a fake handoff. Two other times teams take shots: the first play after a turnover ("sudden change"), and right after a long run, when the linebackers are thinking run.

Why it matters for your bets: totals are built on drive-by-drive scoring. One or two explosive plays can push a low game over. Thursday's Under survived at 46 even with Watson's 53 yards. For Sunday's Chiefs-Broncos Under 40.5, the thing to watch is whether Denver keeps two safeties deep against Patrick Mahomes.

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): Sunday, Ravens at Bills (10:00 a.m., CBS): Lamar Jackson's play-action against Buffalo. Chiefs at Broncos (1:25 p.m., CBS): Mahomes against Denver's safeties. Tonight in college: Ohio State at USC (4:30 p.m., NBC).

Lesson 41: Special teams, the third unit: how a punt gets blocked (and why kicks swung two Big Ten games)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson comes from your Penn State bet: Purdue's only points in a 14-14 first half came from a 33-yard TD pass and a blocked punt returned for a TD.

The big idea: a football team has three units. Offense, defense, and special teams: punts, kickoffs, field goals and extra points.Special teams are only about 1 snap in 6. But a single kick can be worth 7 points with no offense on the field.

White = punting team (LS long snapper, W wings, PP personal protector, P punter, G gunners). Yellow = return team (R rushers, KR returner). The yellow arrow is the free rusher; the yellow X is the block point. Numbers 1–4 match the steps below.

  1. The snap. On 4th down the long snapper (LS) fires the ball about 14 yards back to the punter (P).Snap to kick should take about 2 seconds. Any longer and the rush arrives.
  2. The protection. The linemen and two wings (W) each block one gap.The personal protector (PP), about 5 yards back, is the last blocker. He calls out the protection and takes whoever comes free.
  3. The overload. The return team puts more rushers on one side than the punting team has blockers there.If the protector picks the wrong man, one rusher runs free.
  4. The block point. Rushers don't aim at the punter. They aim about a yard in front of his kicking foot, where the ball will be.A block there sends the ball backward, often to the defense.
  5. Saturday's example. Purdue's Bisi Owens blocked Nathan Tiyce's punt and Jalil Hall scooped it and ran 31 yards for a TD: Penn State 14, Purdue 14 (StateCollege.com).Penn State's offense had been winning (it finished with 269 rushing yards). The block erased a 7-point lead in one play.
  6. The other kicks that mattered. Indiana-Minnesota: Minnesota's Luke Drzewiecki made a 60-yard field goal with 19 seconds left; Indiana's Paddy McAteer answered from 60 as time ran out (ESPN: the first FBS game in at least 30 years with two made 60-yarders). Indiana won in overtime.Penn State's Ryan Barker missed from 55. Last week, Oregon missed three field goals in a loss at Illinois.

How to log it in your drill: on 4th down, first check the formation. A punter 14 yards deep with a personal protector in front of him is a punt, so there's nothing to call. But watch for a fake punt: a direct snap to the protector, or the punter running. Teams fake most on 4th-and-short near midfield, when the return team only has one man deep. Log a fake as RUN (a direct snap) or PASS (the punter throws).

Why it matters for your bets: special-teams TDs, blocked kicks and long field goals are points the offense didn't earn. Totals and margins can't predict them. Purdue's block helped keep your Penn State bet alive at halftime (21-14). The two 60-yarders pushed Indiana-Minnesota into overtime. In today's Chiefs-Broncos Under, the altitude in Denver makes long field goals easier, so drives that stall at the 40 can still score 3.

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): today, Chiefs at Broncos (1:25 p.m., CBS): field goals at altitude. Ravens at Bills (10:00 a.m., CBS). Monday, Bears at Seahawks (5:15 p.m., ESPN). Next Saturday, Penn State at Washington: does Penn State's punt protection hold up?

Lesson 42: Rain and wind: how weather changes the play call (and how to use it in your drill)

Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", with no snaps logged) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: "not configured for this session"). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson comes from Sunday's rain game in Tampa, where one team ran 52 times and threw 3 passes. Weather is a clue you can read before the snap, which is what your drill is about.

The big idea: heavy rain and strong wind shrink the playbook.A wet ball is hard to snap, throw and catch. So offenses run more and throw short.Defenses know it, so they move an extra player close to the line.

White = offense, yellow = defense. A is a normal dry-day call. B is the same formation in heavy rain: one more defender in the box, and the deep pass (crossed out) is rarely called. C is why: the wet ball. D is what happens to the team that falls behind.

  1. A. On a dry day, the whole playbook is open. The defense has to respect the deep pass, so it keeps 7 in the box (Lesson 19).
  2. B. In heavy rain, the deep pass gets risky. The ball slips out of the QB's hand and off receivers' fingers.So the call becomes run, run, short throw. The defense answers with an 8th player in the box.Sunday: Tampa Bay ran 52 times. Bucky Irving had 27 carries for 170 yards and a TD; Kenneth Gainwell 25 for 140. Baker Mayfield threw 3 passes and completed none (NFL.com).
  3. C. The wet ball hurts three things: the snap, the catch and footing.Running backs are less hurt by footing because they run straight ahead. Receivers cut sharply, and that's where they slip.
  4. D. The team that's behind suffers most. It can't run out the clock; it has to throw.Atlanta fell behind, and Michael Penix Jr. threw 24 times: 8 completions, 125 yards, 4 interceptions, a 12.0 rating. Final: Buccaneers 16, Falcons 0.That connects to Lesson 31 (protecting a lead): in rain, a lead is even easier to protect.
  5. Wind is different from rain. Wind hits kicks and deep throws (the ball hangs in the air). Rain hits ball handling.Strong wind: fewer long field goals and deep shots. Heavy rain: more runs, more fumbles and drops.

How to log it in your drill: before the first snap, look at the weather. In heavy rain or strong wind, lean RUN on 1st and 2nd down, especially for the team that's ahead. On 3rd-and-long, still call PASS, but expect a short one. And when a team is behind late in the rain, call PASS: it has no choice.

Why it matters for your bets: more runs mean a running clock, fewer plays and fewer points. Sunday's Bucs-Falcons total was 44.5; the game had 16. Before you buy an Over, or a QB's passing-yards YES, check the forecast. Heavy rain favors the Under and running backs' yards.

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): tonight, Bears at Seahawks (5:15 p.m., ESPN): Lumen Field has no roof. Saturday, Penn State at Washington (12:30 p.m., FS1): Seattle in November; the brief checks the forecast Friday. Next Sunday night, Buccaneers at Bears (5:20 p.m., NBC): Chicago wind.
