Some of that is real; the trouble is that everyone has heard it, so the price may already include it. This lesson is how to tell.

Top: prep days (yellow = this week's Thursday teams). Bottom: white dot = the market's total, yellow dot = points actually scored (or, for this Thursday, CBS SportsLine's projection, dashed). Open white circle = where the Patriots-Bears total opened.

  1. Count the days (top bars). A normal week is 6 days between games. A Monday-night team playing Sunday gets 5 (the 49ers this week, who also fly to Atlanta). A Thursday team gets 3. Coaches say the first thing that goes is the game plan: fewer new plays, more of what the team already does well. Practices are mostly walk-throughs, which is why early-week injury reports for Thursday games say "estimated."
  2. Check whether the rest is equal. This Thursday both teams played at home Sunday, so both have 3 days; New England also travels. A rest gap (one team off a bye, the other off a Monday game) matters more than both teams being equally short.
  3. Look at what's happened (bottom dots). This season's two Thursday games the brief tracked both finished well under the market's total: Bucs-Cowboys 40 points against about 48, Broncos-Seahawks 31 (with overtime) against 40.5. That supports the theory, but two games is a tiny sample: a couple of high-scoring Thursdays would erase it. Treat it as a reason to look, not a reason to bet.
  4. See which way the number moved (bottom row). If the crowd believed "Thursday = Under," the total would drift down. Patriots-Bears did the opposite: it opened 49.5 and is 50.5 now, even though CBS SportsLine's model projects about 44 points and Covers' writer takes the Under. When the total moves up while the sharper sources like the Under, you're getting a slightly better number for the Under than the opener (Lesson 14), which is the good kind of disagreement.
  5. Find the football reason. Rest alone never makes a pick (checklist #2). Here the candidate is New England's offensive line, missing several starters against Chicago's blitz-heavy pass rush: a short week gives a patched-up line less time to practice together. Wednesday's injury report names who's out; that's what turns the lean into a pick or a pass.

Your 30-second check: (1) How many days does each team get, and is it equal? (2) Who travels? (3) Has the total moved, and which way? (4) Is there a specific injury or matchup that a short week makes worse? Only with (4) is it a bet.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 3 and Lesson 14 explain line moves; Lesson 11 (reading injury reports) matters more on a short week, since "estimated" practice reports hide who really practiced; Lesson 17 (key numbers in totals) applies here too: 51 is a common final total, so Under 50.5 loses on exactly 51.

How it played out: Wednesday's report named the injuries (four New England guards gone, three cornerbacks out), and the brief turned the lean into a ¼-unit Under 50.5 pick; result in Friday's edition.

Market 101 · Lesson 29: The bye-week edge: does a week off really make a team better, and is it already in the price?

The idea: every NFL team gets one week off (a "bye"). The popular belief is that a rested team, with two weeks to prepare, plays better the next game, so you should back it. Some of that is true, but the market has known about byes for decades, and the number usually includes it already. This lesson shows what a bye really buys and how to check whether you're paying for it.

Top: days between games (yellow = off a bye). Middle: the four teams coming off the Week 6 bye and their current spreads (Covers, Tue), with the opening number in parentheses. Bottom: two teams' all-time records against the spread after a bye (TeamRankings).

  1. What a bye really buys (top bars). 13 days instead of 6. The biggest benefit isn't "freshness"; it's injured players getting back. Penn State's bye this week is the example: WR Koby Howard and DE LaVar Arrington II were listed out "until after the bye" and could return for Purdue. A team that gets two starters back from a bye has a real, checkable reason; a team that was already healthy mostly just had a week off.
  2. The second benefit: a longer game plan. Coaches get extra days to study one opponent. It helps most when the opponent is on a short week (Lesson 28): the biggest rest gap is a bye team against a team coming off a Monday or Thursday game. None of this week's four bye teams has that gap: the Ravens, Packers, Jets and Colts all played Sunday.
  3. Is it already in the price? (middle rows). The rough market rule of thumb is that rest is worth about a point, not the 3 that home field used to be. Look at this week: the Vikings moved from -5.5 to -6.5 and the Lions from -3 to -3.5, both rested home favorites, so the crowd may already be paying extra for the "rested" story. The Bengals moved toward Baltimore's side only because Lamar Jackson might return (limited Wednesday).
  4. Don't trust team "after a bye" records (bottom line). Denver is 31-16-2 against the spread after a bye; Seattle is 11-28-2. Same week off, opposite results, across many different coaches and rosters. That's what noise looks like: a trend record with no football reason behind it is a coincidence until proven otherwise (checklist #3). The brief made the same point about Michigan "covering 2 of its last 8 after a bye" before the Penn State game: it was a supporting note, not the reason.
  5. Where a bye does show up in bets: when a team returns a key player the market doubted (a starting quarterback, two linemen), or when it faces a team on short rest. Then the bye is the reason (checklist #2), and you can check it on Wednesday's injury report.

Your 30-second check: (1) Who's coming back from injury because of the bye? (2) Is the opponent on short rest? (3) Has the line already moved toward the rested team? (4) If your only reason is "they had a week off," pass.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 28 is the other end of the rest scale (3 days); Lesson 11 (reading injury reports) is how you find who returns; Lesson 16 and Lesson 27 explain why a popular story like "rested team" makes the price worse, not better.

Next: how a quarterback change moves a line (Lamar Jackson and Baker Mayfield both practiced Wednesday).

Market 101 · Lesson 30: Quarterback news: how much a starter moves the line, and when to buy before the decision

The idea: no single player moves a line like a quarterback. When a starter is ruled out, the spread can swing by a touchdown; when his status is unclear, the price sits somewhere in between. This week has five live examples. The lesson is how to read those moves and when the uncertainty itself is the opportunity.

Yellow bars = how many points each line moved from the look-ahead or opening number to Thursday's number (Rotowire, CBS, SI). Bottom: the blend formula for a line whose quarterback is still undecided.

  1. The big move (top bar). Before the season's injuries, Philadelphia was a 3.5-point favorite at home against Dallas. With Jalen Hurts reported out for the season and Tanner McKee starting, Dallas opened -5.5 and sits at -4. That's a 7.5-point swing, more than a touchdown, for one player. A star quarterback replaced by a backup is the biggest single adjustment books make.
  2. Backups aren't all equal (bars 2 and 4). Michigan benched Bryce Underwood for freshman Tommy Carr, and the line moved toward Michigan (Indiana -8.5 to -7): Carr ran for the winning TD against Penn State, and the market liked the change. The Giants lost Jaxson Dart and start J.J. McCarthy, and Houston dropped from -9.5 to -8.5. A backup who has started NFL games costs far less than an unknown.
  3. "Questionable" is a blend (bar 3 and the formula). Lamar Jackson has been limited two days in a row. Baltimore was -3.5 before his injury; with Tyler Huntley it would be closer to a pick'em. Today's -2.5 is the market's blend of both worlds. If Lamar is announced as the starter, expect the number to move back toward -3 or -3.5; if he's out, toward Cincinnati.
  4. Already priced in (bar 5). Baker Mayfield practiced fully Wednesday and Thursday, and Carolina slid only from -3.5 to -3. When a quarterback is practicing fully, the market mostly assumes he plays, so there's little left to gain from "he'll play" news.
  5. When to buy before the decision. If you have a real reason to think a questionable quarterback plays (two full practices, a coach's confident quote), the blended price is a discount: you get "Lamar plays" at a "maybe" price. The risk is the other branch. On Kalshi, a game market settles on the result no matter who starts (Lesson 25: read the rules line), so if he sits, you're simply holding a worse bet. Size it smaller than usual.

Your 30-second check: (1) Who is the backup, and has he started before? (2) Where was the line before the injury, and where is it now? (3) Is the price a blend, i.e., is the starter still undecided? (4) Would you still like the bet if the backup plays? If not, wait for the announcement and accept a worse number.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 11 (reading injury reports) tells you how to judge "limited" vs. "full"; Lesson 14 (following a line) is how you spot the move; Football 101 Lesson 27 explained how an offense shrinks with a backup; today's Football 101 covers what a running quarterback adds, which is exactly what a backup like McKee or Huntley may not have.

Market 101 · Lesson 31: What a total assumes: split it into each team's share (team totals)

The idea: a game total is just two numbers added together, one for each team. The spread tells you how the market splits it. Once you can do the split, you can see which team's scoring a bet depends on, and where Thursday's Under actually broke.

White bars = the favorite's share, yellow = the underdog's, 5 pixels per point; the number after "=" is the total. Shares are worked out with the formula at the bottom (books also post "team totals" close to these: Thursday's were Chicago 26.5, New England 23.5).

  1. The split (bottom of the diagram). Add the spread to the total and halve it for the favorite; subtract and halve for the underdog. Thursday: (50.5 + 3) ÷ 2 = 26.75 for Chicago, (50.5 − 3) ÷ 2 = 23.75 for New England. The books' posted team totals (26.5 and 23.5) were almost exactly that.
  2. Where Thursday broke (rows 1 and 2). New England scored 24, a quarter-point over its share. Chicago scored 30, 3.25 over. So the brief's reason (New England's backup guards would hold its offense down) was about the right team's number being roughly right; the bet lost on Chicago's side, through the cornerback injuries the brief listed as the risk. When you buy a game Under, you're betting on both shares. If your reason is about only one team, a team-total Under on that team is the cleaner bet, when Kalshi or a book offers one.
  3. Ole Miss at Texas (row 3). 54.5 with Texas -3.5 means the market expects about Texas 29, Ole Miss 25.5. That assumes Texas's normal offense. VegasInsider reports Karle Lacy Jr. takes the first-team snaps if Arch Manning doesn't start; if he sits, Texas's 29 is the number that should drop, and with it the spread and the total (Lesson 30: an undecided quarterback makes the price a blend).
  4. Indiana at Michigan (row 4, the brief's pick). 41.5 with Indiana -7 means about Indiana 24, Michigan 17. The Under needs both shares to hold, or one to fall well short. The brief's estimate is Indiana 24, Michigan 13: Indiana right on its share, Michigan 4 short with a freshman making his first start. If you only believed the Michigan part, a Michigan team-total Under would match that belief exactly.
  5. Why running quarterbacks matter to these shares. A quarterback who can run turns broken pass plays into first downs, which keeps drives alive and adds to his team's share. That's the half of Thursday the brief underweighted: Drake Maye ran for a TD and completed 8 of 9 under pressure. A defense's pass rush only lowers the share if the quarterback can't escape it (Football 101, Lesson 33).

Your 30-second check: (1) Split the total with the formula. (2) Ask which team's number your reason is about. (3) If it's one team, look for that team's total instead of the game total. (4) Check what each share assumes about the quarterback.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 1 turned prices into chances; Lesson 9 showed totals break on one-play scores; Lesson 17 covered key totals (41 and 51); Lesson 30 covered quarterback news. This lesson ties them: a total is two teams' expected points, and each one carries its own assumptions.

Market 101 · Lesson 32: Halftime prices: why "on pace for 68" is almost never right

The idea: at halftime, the score makes a game look like it will keep going the same way. Live prices react to that. But second halves don't copy first halves: big first halves usually slow down, and slow ones usually speed up. The skill is telling a real change in the game from a scoreboard that just looks dramatic.

White = first-half points, yellow = second-half points, 3 pixels per point. The dashed yellow line is the "pace" (first half × 2). Bottom row: Hawai'i's game is at halftime as this edition goes out, with its 47.5 pregame total marked in white.

  1. Big first halves slow down (rows 1 and 2). Thursday was 20-14 at the half, 34 points, "on pace for 68." It ended 54: 20 in the second half. Last week's 49ers-Commanders was 20-3 (23 points, pace 46) and ended 40. Two reasons: the team that's ahead runs the ball and lets the clock run (Football 101, Lesson 31: protecting a lead), and a first half often has lucky, fast scores (Thursday's two TDs in the last 14 seconds) that don't repeat.
  2. Slow first halves speed up (row 3). Penn State led Michigan 3-0 at the half. Michigan changed quarterbacks, and the second half had 36 points. A live Under bought at halftime "because it's 3-0" would have been buying the scoreboard, not the game.
  3. What the live price really is. A halftime total = points already scored + the market's guess for the second half. Thursday at the half, a fair live total was about 34 + 20 to 24 = 54 to 58, not 68. If a live Over is priced as if the pace will hold, that's the overreaction from Lesson 8, and the cheap side is usually the Under.
  4. When a halftime price IS a deal: the reason changed. A quarterback benched or hurt (Michigan's switch to Tommy Carr last week), a key injury, a weather change, or a big yardage gap that the score hasn't caught up to. Hawai'i today: 35-14 with 351 yards to 150 and 17 first downs to 6. That lead is backed by the yards (the Oct 3 lesson: trust yards per play over an early score). Tennessee was down 14-0 after one quarter at South Carolina and led 21-17 at halftime: a score that wasn't backed by much.
  5. Pregame bets and halftime. Any pregame Over 47.5 in Hawai'i-NIU has already cashed (49 points). For a live bet, the only question is the second half. With a 21-point lead, the likely script is Hawai'i running clock, so second-half points will probably come in under the first half's 49.

Your 30-second halftime check: (1) Do the pace math, then knock it down for a big first half (up for a slow one). (2) Ask what changed besides the score: quarterback, injury, weather, yards. (3) Compare yards per play with the score. (4) If nothing changed, don't chase the scoreboard.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 8 introduced live overreactions; Lesson 9 showed totals break on one-play scores; Lesson 31 split a total into each team's share. Halftime is where all three meet: the score so far, the one-play swings, and which team still needs points.

Market 101 · Lesson 33: Monday night: the last game of the week, and a line that moved 9 points

The idea: the Monday-night game is the last bet of the football week. It has the most information behind it (every injury report is final, every other result is in) and the most emotion around it (by Monday you know whether your weekend is up or down). Tonight's Cowboys at Eagles line shows where the value in a line actually comes from, and when it's already gone.

White dots = earlier prices, yellow = now. Yellow dashed lines = key numbers (the most common final margins and totals). Spread numbers from the brief's Week 7 table (look-ahead from sportsbrackets.net, open from SI/DraftKings, now from VegasInsider); totals from VegasInsider.

  1. Most of the move happened before the week started (top row). The look-ahead line, posted a week early, had Philadelphia -3.5. Then the Eagles lost a fourth straight game, Jalen Hurts went on injured reserve (blood clots), and Tanner McKee became the starter. When the week's betting opened, Dallas was -5.5: a 9-point swing (3.5 to pick'em, plus 5.5 more). That's Lesson 14 again: lines move most when news breaks, and only someone holding the earlier number got that value. By Monday, the quarterback news is the least valuable information in the building.
  2. Since the open: one point back. Dallas -4.5 now (HardRock -5), moneyline Dallas -218 to -230 / Philadelphia +180. Barkley's full practice Saturday and money on the home underdog pulled it back. Notice where it sits: between the key numbers 3 and 7. Few NFL games end on a 4-point margin, so moving from Dallas -4.5 to -3.5 is a cheap step; moving across 3 or 7 is expensive (Lessons 2 and 20). If you liked Dallas, -4.5 is a fine number; if you liked Philadelphia, +4.5 doesn't cover a 7-point Dallas win, the most important number past 3.
  3. The total tells the same story (bottom row). 48.5 → 44.5 at the books, 43.5 at Kalshi and DraftKings, sitting right on the key total 44 (Lesson 17). Split it (Lesson 31): 44 with Dallas -4.5 means about Dallas 24, Philadelphia 20. The drop came almost entirely out of Philadelphia's share, which is what a backup quarterback does.
  4. Monday has the most information, so waiting is often free. Barkley is questionable; the price already blends "he plays" and "he sits" (Lesson 30). If you don't know which, you have no edge, and the answer comes about 90 minutes before kickoff (inactives Mon 3:45 p.m. PT; the brief checks it). The bet worth watching is the overreaction: if he's ruled out and the line jumps 1.5 points or more, that's a market paying too much for a running back.
  5. The last-game trap. By Monday you know your weekend net, and "one more bet to get even" is the most expensive bet of the week. Your Oct 1–5 weekend had one: a live Bijan 160+ bought right after a long TD, which lost $20, more than the other two Monday bets made together. Rule: Monday's bet has to pass the checklist on its own, sized from your weekly budget (Lesson 24), never from what you're down.
  6. Trends describe; prices predict. "Philadelphia is 1-5 against the spread and 0-3 at home" is true and already known by everyone setting the line. It's a tiebreaker at most (checklist #4), never the reason.

Your 30-second Monday check: (1) Where did the line start (look-ahead), and has the big news already moved it? (2) Is it sitting next to 3 or 7? (3) What's still undecided (a questionable star), and can you wait for it? (4) Would you make this bet if it were Thursday and your week were even?

Connecting the dots: Lesson 14 followed a line from open to kickoff; Lesson 30 priced quarterback news; Lesson 31 split totals; Lesson 24 set a weekly budget. Monday night uses all four, plus one more skill: not letting the weekend's results choose the bet.

Next: Thursday-night openers: how the first number of the week is set, using Panthers at Packers.

Market 101 · Lesson 34: Thursday-night openers: how the first number of the week is set (Panthers at Packers)

The idea: every NFL week starts with a number posted before almost anyone has bet: the opener. It's the least-tested price of the week, and by Thursday's kickoff it has been pushed around by days of betting into the most-tested one, the close. Knowing which stage you're buying at tells you how much to trust the number. This week's Thursday game, Panthers at Packers (Thu Oct 29, 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video), shows every stage.

Top: the three stages of the Thursday line (white = earlier, yellow = the close). Bottom: the share of NFL games decided by exactly each margin, rounded, approximate long-run figures to show the shape; 3 and 7 stand out. Lines from Covers' Week 8 board (Oct 26).

  1. Stage 1, the opener (Sunday night). A few books post the next week's lines within hours of Sunday's games ending, starting from their own power ratings and the look-ahead line (Lesson 14). This one: Green Bay -3.5, total 47.5. Books take only small bets at this stage (low limits, the short bar on the left), because they know the number is a first draft.
  2. Stage 2, the first bets (Monday to Wednesday). Professional bettors hit the numbers they think are wrong, and the books move. By Monday some books were at -4.5, with totals spread from 46.5 to 48. Notice the reason: Carolina just lost 43-13 at home with 4 turnovers, while Green Bay lost a 3-point game at Detroit. A blowout moves bettors more than it should; the score was mostly turnovers (Lessons 16 and 27: what the public's money does to a line). That's the half-point the brief is watching.
  3. Stage 3, the close (Thursday kickoff). Limits are at their highest, injury reports are final, and the most money has tested the number. That's why "did you beat the close?" (the closing-price tracker under How picks are made) is the best quick test of a bet (Lesson 6): buying a better number than the close, over many bets, is what winning bettors do.
  4. Why -3.5 to -4.5 is a "cheap" move (bottom chart). About 15% of NFL games end on exactly 3 points and about 9% on exactly 7; only about 5% end on exactly 4. Moving from -3.5 to -4.5 only adds the 4-point games, so if you like Carolina, +4.5 is a little better than +3.5, not a lot. Crossing 3 (from -2.5 to -3.5) is the expensive move: that's where half-points cost real money (Lessons 2 and 20).
  5. Short week for both. Both teams played Sunday, so neither has a rest edge (Lesson 28: rest matters most when only one team has it). Home field in the NFL is now worth about 1.5 points, so -3.5 says the books rate Green Bay about 2 points better on a neutral field.
  6. On Kalshi. Thursday markets open early but trade thin until game day: the gap between the buy and sell price is wide. Use a limit order (set your price) instead of tapping the first price shown, and compare to the books' line before you buy.

When to bet early vs. wait: if your side is the one the market is moving toward (Green Bay this week), early is better: the number only gets worse. If your side is the other one (Carolina), waiting is often free: the half-point may come to you. If you don't know yet, wait for the injury report (Wednesday evening PT).

Your 30-second Thursday check: (1) What's the opener, and which way has it moved? (2) Did a key number (3 or 7) get crossed? (3) Is the move about news, or about one ugly score? (4) Will you beat the closing number by buying now?

Connecting the dots: Lesson 14 followed a line from open to close; Lesson 20 priced each half-point; Lesson 28 covered short weeks; Lesson 33 showed a Monday line where the news had already moved everything. Thursday is the other end of the week: the least information, the softest number.

Next: player props on Thursday: how a yardage line is set, and why backup-quarterback games are hard to price.

Market 101 · Lesson 35: Player props: how a yardage line is set, and why backup-quarterback games are hard to price

The idea: a prop like "Jordan Love: over/under 239.5 passing yards" isn't the book's guess at his average game. It's the middle game: the number he goes over about half the time. That small difference explains why ladder rungs far above the line are long shots, why props on backup quarterbacks are coin flips with wide misses, and why Monday night's two un-counted props both won (Tanner McKee 200+ yards; Saquon Barkley under 17.5 carries).

Bars: how often a typical starting quarterback lands in each 25-yard range (an illustrative shape). Yellow line (1) = where the book sets the over/under; dashed line (2) = the average; the boxes (3) are Kalshi's one-market-per-rung ladder. Numbers match the steps below.

  1. The starting projection. A book (and the traders who move Kalshi) starts from expected pass attempts × yards per attempt, then adjusts for the opponent and the script. Love threw 45 times for 274 yards at Detroit, but Green Bay was behind most of that game. Thursday it's a 3.5-point favorite, and teams that lead run more (Lesson 31), so a fair line sits below 274. That's why Football Nation's "worth a look" number for Love is 239.5 or lower.
  2. The line is the middle game, not the average (yellow vs. dashed). Yards pile up unevenly: a bad day can't go below zero, but one 60-yard catch-and-run adds 60. The few big games pull the average to the right, while the middle game (the median) stays put. The book sets its line at the middle, so the over and under each win about half the time. If you judge an over by a player's season average, you'll think it's cheaper than it is.
  3. The ladder (bottom boxes). Kalshi lists one market per rung: "200+ passing yards," "250+," and so on (Lesson 15). The rung closest to the book's line trades near 50¢; each rung above it gets cheaper faster than it looks, because it lives out in the thin right tail. Before you buy a rung, find the book's over/under and ask: is my rung above or below it?
  4. Why backup quarterbacks are hard to price. The projection needs a track record. Monday's Tanner McKee had one start (14 points), so the market had little to go on and priced "McKee: 200+ passing yards" at 50¢: a coin flip because nobody knew. He threw for 211. With a backup, the true range is wide in both directions, and his receivers' props inherit the same fog (Makai Lemon had 7 catches for 67). The brief's rule: with a backup, a 50¢ prop is only a bet when there's a specific reason (a defense that can't cover, a game script that forces throws), not because the price looks "fair."
  5. The injury exit. SI's Monday pick, Barkley under 17.5 carries, won by 10.5 because Barkley left with a back injury after 7 carries. Unders on carries and yards quietly carry that edge: if the player gets hurt or pulled in a blowout, the under wins. Overs carry the opposite risk. If a player doesn't play at all, what happens to the bet depends on the market: read its rules line before you buy (Lesson 25).
  6. Thursday timing. Thursday props post late and trade thin; FanDuel's Panthers-Packers board was still empty Sunday night. Wait for the books' line, then set a limit price on Kalshi rather than tapping the first price (Lesson 34).

Your 30-second prop check: (1) What's the books' over/under, and is your rung above or below it? (2) Is the player's team likely to lead or trail (more runs or more throws)? (3) Is the quarterback a backup (wide range, no edge from price alone)? (4) Over or under, who wins if he gets hurt?

Connecting the dots: Lesson 15 built the yardage ladder; Lesson 27 (Football 101) showed how a backup shrinks the game plan; Lesson 31 split a total by team; this lesson sets the center of a single player's number. Thursday's edition applies it to the Panthers-Packers props when they post.

Next: Sunday-night lines with a backup quarterback: how far a market moves when the starter and the top running back are both out (Eagles at Commanders).

Market 101 · Lesson 36: When a team loses its quarterback and then its top running back: how far a line moves (Eagles at Commanders)

The idea: a point spread is the market's estimate of the gap between two teams. When players get hurt, it moves, but not every player moves it the same amount. Sunday night's Eagles at Commanders (Sun Nov 1, 5:20 p.m. PT, NBC) has moved three times in two weeks, and splitting the move into pieces shows how the market values a quarterback, a running back and a crowd of smaller injuries.

Top: the spread on one line, Philadelphia favored on the left, Washington on the right; the three dots (1–3) are the three prices, brackets A and B are the pieces of the move, yellow ticks are the key numbers 3 and 7. Bottom (C): the total on the look-ahead line vs. this week. Numbers match the steps below.

  1. Three prices (dots 1–3). Before Week 7, the look-ahead line had Philadelphia -2.5, total 46.5. After Monday's 38-21 loss at Dallas it opened Washington -3.5, total 40.5 (Covers). By Wednesday it was Washington -5.5 (-108), Eagles +5.5 (-112), moneyline -218 / +180, total still 40.5 (DraftKings via SI). That's 8 points on the spread and 6 on the total.
  2. Piece A, about 6 points: the quarterback (plus results). Jalen Hurts went on IR and Tanner McKee became the starter; Philadelphia also lost a fifth straight game. A starting quarterback is the only position that routinely moves a line 3 to 7 points by himself (Lesson 30), and this one landed in the middle of that range. Five straight losses and Monday's 17-point beating added a little more.
  3. Piece B, about 2 points: everything else. From Monday to Wednesday: Saquon Barkley hurt his back Monday, Dameon Pierce left too, and both are questionable with WR DeVonta Smith; RT Lane Johnson is out. A single non-quarterback is rarely worth more than a point to the market; Barkley alone isn't 2 points. A 2-point move says the market is pricing several missing pieces at once, plus money coming in on Washington, which is off its bye.
  4. The key-number check (yellow ticks). Moving from 3.5 to 5.5 passes 4 and 5, not 3 or 7 (Lesson 34). About 5% of NFL games end on 4 and about 4% on 5, so an Eagles bettor gets roughly 9% more winning outcomes at +5.5 than at +3.5: real, but less than "2 points" sounds. Crossing 7 (to -7.5) would be the expensive move.
  5. Piece C: why the total moved with the quarterback, not the back. A backup quarterback means shorter drives, more punts and a leading opponent that runs the clock, so both teams score less: the total dropped 6 points when Hurts went out. A running back changes who carries the ball more than how many points get scored, so the total sat still at 40.5 through the Barkley news.
  6. Buying before the news. Barkley says he hurt his back compensating for his hamstring and doesn't expect to miss time (Bleacher Report). If he's cleared, this line can drift back toward 4.5; if he's ruled out, 6.5 is possible. Buying Eagles +5.5 now is partly a bet that he sits; buying Washington -5.5 is a bet that he doesn't matter. SI's pick is Eagles +5.5, citing Washington's 31st-ranked run defense by opponent success rate, which only helps if a healthy back is carrying the ball. On Kalshi the same bet reads "Washington wins by over 5.5 points" → NO.

Your 30-second injury-move check: (1) Is the player a quarterback (big move) or anyone else (small, unless several are out together)? (2) Did the move cross 3 or 7? (3) Did the total move too (QB news) or only the spread? (4) Is the player's status still open, and which way will the line go when it's decided?

Connecting the dots: Lesson 30 sized a starting quarterback; Lesson 33 watched a Monday line move 9 points on quarterback news; Lesson 34 priced half-points around 3 and 4; this lesson splits one move into its pieces. Friday's edition re-checks this line after the Eagles' Thursday practice report.

Next: Thursday-night results vs. the closing number: what the Panthers-Packers close says about the brief's Under, win or lose.

Market 101 · Lesson 37: Totals have key numbers too: why 40.5 and 41.5 are different bets (and how Thursday's Under graded)

The idea: a total (over/under) is a bet on the two teams' combined points. Football points come in 3s and 7s, so some combined scores happen more often than others. When a total sits right next to one of those common scores, half a point decides a lot of bets.

The line is combined points. Yellow ticks: common final totals (37, 41, 44, 47). Dashed markers: the two lines the brief bet this week. A, B and C match the steps below.

  1. Why some totals are common. Touchdowns are worth 7 and field goals 3, so totals built from them (like 24 + 17 = 41, 20 + 17 = 37, 27 + 17 = 44, 27 + 20 = 47) come up again and again.Each of the common ones lands in roughly 1 NFL game in 20. That's much smaller than the 3 in a point spread (about 15% of games), but it's real.
  2. A. Sunday's Under 40.5. The brief's Chiefs-Broncos Under wins at 40 or fewer.B. The danger is 41, one of the common totals. These teams' Week 1 game ended 31-10: exactly 41.At 41.5 that game is a win; at 40.5 it's a loss. The total moved from 42.5 to 40.5 this week, and the move crossed 41, the expensive number.
  3. What that means for price. Losing a common total is worth a few cents.That's why the brief caps this pick at 52¢ instead of the 55¢ it might pay at 41.5. If Kalshi shows a "Total points over 41.5" market, its NO side at 46–47¢ or less is the better buy.
  4. C. Grading Thursday. Packers 27, Panthers 19 is 46 points, so Under 47.5 won by 1.5.47 was next door: a successful Carolina 2-point try in the 4th quarter makes it 48 and a loss. The result was a little lucky.The better grade is the price: the brief bought at 47.5, and the last line it saw before kickoff was still 47.5. Even against the close: the pick wasn't beaten by the market, but it didn't beat it either (Lesson 6).

Your 30-second totals check: (1) What's the line? (2) Is 37, 41, 44 or 47 right next to it? (3) Are you on the good side of that number? (4) If not, look for the next line on Kalshi's ladder, or pay less.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 34 priced half-points around the spread's key numbers 3 and 7; Lesson 36 split a line move into pieces. This lesson does the same for totals, where the key numbers are smaller but still worth checking before every Under or Over.

Next: grading Sunday's Under against its closing number, win or lose.

Market 101 · Lesson 38: Key margins: why 14 sank "wins by over 13.5" (your Penn State bet)

The idea: a "wins by over X" market is a bet on the final margin.Points come in 3s and 7s, so some margins happen far more often than others.When one of those common margins sits right above your line, half a point decides a lot of bets.

Bar heights are rough shares of college final margins (exact numbers vary by season and source). Tall bars: 3, 7, 10, 14 and 17. The yellow bar is 14, Saturday's Penn State margin. The dashed line is your bet's line, 13.5. A, B and C match the steps below.

  1. Why some margins are common. A field goal is 3. A touchdown is 7. Two touchdowns is 14.So 3, 7, 10 (TD + FG), 14 and 17 come up again and again. In college, each of 3, 7 and 14 lands in roughly 1 game in 20 or more.In the NFL the bunching is stronger: 3 alone is about 15% of games (Lesson 34).
  2. A. Your bet. "Penn St. wins by over 13.5" → NO wins if Penn State wins by 13 or fewer, or loses.B. Penn State won 31-17: exactly 14. Two touchdowns, the most common big margin, and the one number right above your line.A NO at "over 14.5" wins every game yours wins, plus the 14s.
  3. C. What the half point is worth. If about 1 college game in 20 ends at exactly 14, the 14.5 line is worth about 5¢ more than 13.5.So: if Kalshi's "over 14.5" NO costs less than about 5¢ more than the 13.5 NO, buy the 14.5.At 13 (rare) the half point is worth almost nothing. At 14 it's worth a lot. Same half point, different price.
  4. D. Live bets move in jumps. You bought at about 14-7. From a 7-point lead, the most likely next score for a team running at 9 yards a carry is another TD: 21-7, a 14-point lead.Live, ask "what does one more score do?" A 7-point lead is one TD from 14. A 10-point lead is one FG from 13, or one TD from 17.
  5. How it played out. Purdue tied it 14-14 (blocked punt). Penn State went 21-14, 24-14, then 31-14. Purdue's late field goal made it 31-17.One more Purdue field goal (or Ryan Barker's miss from 55 going in) moves the margin off 14, one way or the other. That's how thin these bets are.

Your 30-second margin check: (1) What's the line? (2) Is 3, 7, 10, 14 or 17 right above it (for a NO) or right below it (for a YES)? (3) If yes, look one step up Kalshi's ladder and compare prices. (4) Pay up to about 5¢ for the half point over 3, 7 or 14.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 34 priced the half points around 3 and 7 in NFL spreads. Lesson 37 did the same for totals (37, 41, 44, 47). This lesson is the same idea for "wins by over" markets, where 14 is the big one that bettors forget.

Next: grading today's Chiefs-Broncos Under against its closing number, win or lose.

Market 101 · Lesson 39: Grade the price, not just the result: two Sunday Unders and their closing numbers

The idea: every bet gets two grades.The result: did it win? The price: did you get a better number than the market's last one before kickoff (the "close")?Results are noisy. Over many bets, the price grade tells you more about whether the picks are good.

A is where the bet was bought. B is the close, the last number before kickoff. C is the final score's total. Yellow marks the close. Both lines run from 36 to 54 points.

  1. What "the close" means. By kickoff, the line has absorbed every injury report and every big bet. It's the market's best guess.If you bought a better number than the close, you "beat the close" (Lesson 6). Bettors who do that often tend to win over time, even through losing weeks.
  2. Chiefs-Broncos, price. A: the brief bought Under 40.5. B: the total closed at 41.5 (theScore, FOX).An Under at 41.5 wins everything 40.5 wins, plus a 41. So the close was the better Under. The brief's number was a point worse: no on price.
  3. Chiefs-Broncos, result. C: 52 points. Over by 11.5.This wasn't a half-point loss. The read was wrong: Mahomes threw for 321 and 3 TDs against a defense the brief thought would bother him.Bad price and bad result together say: the market moved the other way for a reason. Lesson: when the number moves against you before kickoff, re-check the case.
  4. Your Eagles-Commanders Under. A and B: you bought 40.5, and it closed at 40.5. Even on price.C: 37. Won by 3.5.Even on price means you paid a fair number, about 51¢ for a coin flip. The win came from the read: Philadelphia scored 10, all in the 1st quarter.
  5. The brief's record on price. Of its last 10 picks in the closing-price tracker, 7 beat the close at least slightly, 2 were even, and Sunday's was the only "no".That's a good sign for the process, even in a 1-1 week. The best edges came from buying early, when the reason was new (an injury) and before the market moved.

Your 30-second price check: (1) Write down your number when you buy. (2) Look at the line just before kickoff. (3) Is the close better for your side, worse, or the same? (4) Keep the tally. Over 20 bets, "beat the close" matters more than "won".

Connecting the dots: Lesson 6 introduced the closing line. Lesson 37 showed why 41 is a key total, so 40.5 vs. 41.5 is a real difference. This lesson grades two real bets with both tools.

Next: tonight's Bears +3.5 against its close, and why buying +3.5 on Kalshi beats +3 at a book.

Market 101 · Lesson 40: What a quarterback is worth: the 12-point Ravens swing (and why you shop the number)

The idea: a point spread is the market's guess at the final margin.When a star quarterback goes down, that guess moves more than for any other player.Thursday's Jaguars-Ravens line shows how much, and why the same bet can cost different numbers at different places.

The line runs from Baltimore favored by 4 (left) to Jacksonville favored by 10 (right). A, B and C are the three prices in the text. Yellow ticks mark the key margins 3, 7 and 10.

  1. A. Before the injury: Ravens -3, total 48.5. That was the look-ahead line, posted a week early (CBS).Baltimore at home with Lamar Jackson was a field-goal favorite.
  2. B. After: Jaguars -7.5 to -8.5, total 43.5. Lamar hurt his thumb on Baltimore's first snap at Buffalo. He's on IR.Backup Tyler Huntley hurt a toe in the same game. So the Ravens may start their third QB, Joe Fagnano.
  3. C. Monday: Jaguars -9.5, total 42.5 at the book Covers tracks.From A to C, the line moved about 12.5 points. Not all of that is Lamar. Part is Huntley too, and part is the Jaguars' 42-7 win on Sunday.
  4. Why so many points? A quarterback touches the ball on every pass play. An elite one is usually worth several points on his own; most other players are worth 1 or less.Here the drop is from an MVP-level starter to a third-stringer: Fagnano went 10 of 21 for 91 yards and an interception in relief.
  5. The total moves too. A backup QB means fewer points for his team. 48.5 became 42.5: 6 points.That's why the brief won't bet the Under here: the news is already in the price.
  6. Shop the number. On Tuesday, DraftKings had Jaguars -7.5 (SI). Another book had -9.5.-7.5 wins on an 8- or 9-point Jacksonville win. -9.5 loses both. Two points around 7 and 10 are worth a lot.On Kalshi, find "Jacksonville wins by over 7.5". Don't settle for "over 9.5" if both are listed.

Your 30-second injury check: (1) Who's out: the QB, or someone else? (2) Write down the line before and after the news. (3) Has the total moved too? (4) Before you buy, compare at least two prices for the same margin.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 11 showed which injury tags move a line. Lesson 34 priced the key margins 3 and 7. Lesson 39 graded bets against the close. This lesson puts them together on one real line move.

Next: Thursday's lean against its closing price, and what happened to the number after the injury report.

Market 101 · Lesson 41: When the line runs away: Jaguars -7.5 became -10 (what a missed number costs)

The idea: news moves a line fast.If you had a reason to bet before the news, the good number only exists before it.Thursday's Jaguars-Ravens line moved 2 to 3 points in one afternoon. Here is what those points are worth.

Bars show roughly how often an NFL game ends with each winning margin. A, B and C are the three Jaguars lines in the text. The yellow bars are the margins you lose by moving from -7.5 to -9.5.

  1. A. Tuesday morning: Jaguars -7.5 at DraftKings (SI).The brief's lean: "Jacksonville wins by over 7.5" → YES at 52¢ or less.Its reason: Baltimore's third QB would likely start.
  2. The news. Tuesday, coach Jesse Minter named undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano the starter (ESPN).Backup Tyler Huntley went to IR with season-ending turf toe (Athlon). The new backup, Kedon Slovis, came off Green Bay's practice squad.
  3. B. Tuesday afternoon: Jaguars -9.5 at FanDuel, Fanatics, BetRivers and bet365. -10 at BetMGM and Hard Rock.C. Jaguars -10.5 at DraftKings (WinDaily, FOX).The total fell from 43.5 to 40.5. Kalshi now lists "Jacksonville wins by over 9.5" at 53¢.
  4. What 2 points cost. -7.5 wins if Jacksonville wins by 8 or 9. -9.5 loses both.Wins by exactly 8 or 9 happen in roughly 6 of every 100 NFL games (the yellow bars).So the same bet at -9.5 is worth about 6¢ less. The brief rated "over 7.5" about 55%. That makes "over 9.5" about 49%.
  5. Why 10 matters too. 10 is the third most common margin, after 3 and 7 (Lesson 34)."Over 9.5" wins on a 10-point win. DraftKings' -10.5 does not. Shopping still matters after the move.
  6. Was the brief right? The market moved toward its lean: that is "beating the close" (Lesson 39), a good sign for the read.But a lean you didn't buy pays nothing. And chasing it at 53¢ means paying more than the brief thinks it's worth.So: no bet. That is the cap doing its job.

Your news-move check: (1) Is my reason a coming announcement (a QB, a star's status)? (2) If yes, buy before it, with a limit order at my cap. (3) If the line already moved, re-price it: count the margins I lost. (4) Above my cap, skip. No chasing.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 40 showed why a QB moves a line so much. Lesson 34 priced the key margins. Lesson 39 graded bets against the close. This lesson adds the cost of being late.

Next: Thursday's closing number, and how the final margin landed against -7.5, -9.5 and -10.5.

Market 101 · Lesson 42: Team totals: betting one team's points (tonight's Ravens 14.5)

The idea: a team total is an over/under on one team's points, not both.Tonight's Kalshi market: "Jacksonville at Baltimore: Baltimore over 14.5 points."YES wins if the Ravens score 15 or more. NO wins at 14 or fewer. Overtime counts.

Bars show roughly how often an NFL team ends a game on each score. A is tonight's line. B (yellow) is where NO wins; C (white) is where YES wins.

  1. Find the books' number. Take the game total, subtract the spread, and divide by 2. That's the underdog's points.Tonight: (39.5 − 10) ÷ 2 = 14.75 for Baltimore. The Jaguars get the rest: 24.75 (VegasInsider).Kalshi's two team totals match: Baltimore 14.5, Jacksonville 24.5.
  2. A. The line sits between 14 and 15.14 is a common NFL score (two touchdowns). 15 is rare (1.5%). So 14.5 is a good spot for the Under: a 14 counts for NO.
  3. B and C. Count the scores on each side. 10, 13 and 14 sit just below. 17 and 20 sit just above.The question is whether Baltimore gets to 17: two touchdowns plus a field goal.Its last three games: 10, 13 and 10. Fagnano's relief work: 10 of 21, 91 yards, 1 INT.
  4. Price it. Kalshi: "Baltimore over 14.5" YES 46¢ / NO 55¢. So the market gives NO about 55%.The brief gives NO about 57%. That's a 2-point edge. Thin, so the cap (55¢) is firm.
  5. Why a team total, not the spread? The spread needs Jacksonville to win by 10+. That depends on the Jaguars' offense too.The Ravens' team total only asks one question: can a rookie QB lead three scoring drives? It isolates the reason for the bet (Lesson 40: what a QB is worth).
  6. The catch: defense and special teams count. A pick-six by Baltimore's defense or a punt-return TD adds 7 to Baltimore's total.So do late points when the game is decided (Lesson 31 on protecting a lead).

Your team-total check: (1) Work out the books' number: (total − spread) ÷ 2. (2) Find where the line sits: just below 14, 17, 20, 24 or 27 is good for the Over; just above them is good for the Under. (3) Ask what has to happen: how many drives reach the end zone? (4) Price it against your cap.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 37 showed key numbers for game totals. Lesson 40 priced a QB. Lesson 41 showed the cost of a moved line. Tonight's team total uses all three.

Next: how tonight's Ravens total and the Jaguars spread graded against their closing prices.

Market 101 · Lesson 43: Grading Thursday: a win, the closing price, and the bet the brief skipped

The idea: every bet gets two grades.Grade 1: did it win? That's luck plus skill.Grade 2: was the price good? Compare your number with the closing number (Lesson 39). That's mostly skill.Over many bets, Grade 2 predicts your profit better than Grade 1.

A = the line you bought. B = what the closing books implied. C = the final. D, E and F do the same for the Jaguars spread the brief skipped.

  1. A and B: the price. You bought "Baltimore over 14.5 points" → NO at 55¢.At kickoff the books had about Jaguars -10, total 39.5. Lesson 42's math: (39.5 − 10) ÷ 2 = 14.75 Ravens points.14.5 vs. 14.75 is a quarter point. So the price was about even with the close. Not a steal, not a mistake.
  2. C: the result. Baltimore scored 10. You won $3.81 on $5.The reason held: Joe Fagnano threw for 60 yards. Baltimore's only points before garbage time were a field goal.
  3. Even a win had a scare. Justice Hill's 65-yard TD run came at 33-3. That's the "garbage time" risk the card named.One more field goal would still have won. One more touchdown would have lost. A 4-point cushion is normal for a team total.
  4. D and E: the skipped lean. Tuesday the brief liked Jaguars -7.5. By Wednesday the line was -10. The brief skipped it (Lesson 41: don't chase).F: the Jaguars won by 23. Both -7.5 and -10 would have won.
  5. So was skipping wrong? No. At -10 the brief rated it about 49%. Over 100 bets like that, you lose money, even if this one won.The useful lesson is about timing: the edge was real on Tuesday. Bet earlier when the reason is a known QB change (Lesson 41).

Your grading check after every bet: (1) Write down your line and price. (2) Find the closing line. (3) Did you beat it, match it, or miss it? (4) Then look at the result. (5) Count both grades over 20+ bets before changing anything.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 39 introduced the closing line. Lesson 41 showed the cost of being late. Lesson 42 built the team-total number. Today uses all three on one real bet.

Next: Saturday's Oregon-Ohio State market, and what happens when the total moves above your number.

Patriots 29, Bills 26 (your combo leg: lost)

  • Pregame: Buffalo -6.5, ~74%. 12:20 forecast: Patriots 24-20, Bills ~38%. The winner was right; it was a lot wilder.
  • 4th quarter: a Bills field goal made it 21-20.Then Josh Allen hit Keon Coleman for a 34-yard TD with 4:33 left: Bills 26-21, but the 2-point try failed.Drake Maye answered with a 23-yard TD to Efton Chism with 1:55 left, plus a 2-point catch: Patriots 29-26.
  • Why New England won: it had the ball 34 minutes to 26, outgained Buffalo 405-340, and Maye threw 3 TDs.The brief flagged New England's running game early; it kept Buffalo's offense off the field all day.

Chiefs 30, Raiders 27 (your Raiders +5.5 and the brief's +4.5: won)

  • Pregame: KC -4.5. Brief said the Raiders' pass rush and home field would keep it close.
  • How it went: Raiders led 13-10 at half and 19-17 with 5 minutes left.Kansas City then scored two TDs in 15 seconds of game clock (both by Kenneth Walker, the second a 22-yard run): 30-19.A Kirk Cousins TD to Brock Bowers plus a 2-point catch made it 30-27 with 1:46 left, so both +4.5 and +5.5 covered.The onside kick failed.
  • The real story: Las Vegas outgained KC 437-399 and Cousins threw for 365, but four drives ended in field goals instead of TDs.The pass rush the brief liked got 2 sacks; the Chiefs ran for 7.3 yards a carry.

49ers 24, Broncos 14 (Broncos +2.5/+3 and Over 48.5: lost)

  • Pregame: SF -3, total 46.5. Brief's reason for Denver: San Francisco, missing three pass rushers, would have to blitz and give up big plays.
  • What happened: the 49ers got zero sacks, but Denver never hit a big play either.Bo Nix threw 42 times for just 214 yards; Denver's passes traveled only 34 yards in the air total, almost all short throws.The game was 3-3 at half, which sank the over early.
  • The finish: SF led 17-6; Nix found Jaylen Waddle for a TD plus 2 points to make it 17-14 with 4:10 left (Broncos +3 alive).Then Brock Purdy hit George Kittle for 56 yards.49ers 24-14.
  • Brief's miss: the read on the 49ers' pass rush was right, but it assumed Denver would take deep shots.It didn't.Lesson for the brief: a weak pass rush only matters if the other offense throws deep.

Seahawks 30, Chargers 23 (combo leg ✓; Smith-Njigba bets lost)

  • Pregame: SEA -7.5. Brief expected Seattle to lead and keep throwing to Smith-Njigba.
  • What happened: Seattle led 30-13 but ran instead (138 rushing yards), so Smith-Njigba had 5 catches for 76 yards, 4 short of the brief's 80 and 24 short of your 100.Seattle's two TD catches went to Eric Wilson and Tory Horton.The Chargers turned it over 4 times; 30 penalties combined slowed everything down.Uchenna Nwosu's strip-sack with 54 seconds left sealed it.

Other combo legs

  • Ravens 24, Titans 18 ✓ (12:20 forecast 31-13). Baltimore didn't score after halftime; Tennessee's 8 fourth-quarter points made it closer, but the leg won.
  • Vikings 15, Dolphins 10 ✓ A grind, as the 38.5 total suggested. Minnesota won but didn't cover 9.5.
  • Colts 30, Commanders 13 ✓ (morning game).

Sunday night: Panthers 32, Lions 26

  • Pregame: DET -3.5, total 50.5, Lions ~65%. Result: Carolina won outright, and 58 points went over.
  • How: Bryce Young was 29 of 41 for 329 yards and 2 TDs, both to rookie Tetairoa McMillan (32 and 10 yards).Chuba Hubbard ran for 2 TDs.Carolina gained 445 yards, held the ball for 33 minutes, and had zero turnovers.
  • Detroit's problem: Jared Goff threw for 412 yards, but the Lions ran only 15 times (46 yards) and kept stalling near the goal line: 4 field goals and just 2 TDs on 11 red-zone pass attempts.Field goals instead of touchdowns is how a team outgains its opponent and still loses (same story as the Raiders on Sunday).
  • The brief's conditional over: Carolina played without CBs Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, the exact trigger for buying Over 50.5.The check wasn't done, so no bet was signaled.It would have won.
